question:
Question: Cram Session
Costs 1 colorless and 1 B or G. If I tap one swamp and one forest, does this count as casting both a black and green spell?
[[Cram Session]]
answer:
No, tapping one swamp and one forest does not count as casting both a black and green spell. Cram Session has a hybrid mana cost of {C}{B/G}, which means it can be paid with either one colorless mana and one black mana, or one colorless mana and one green mana. The cost does not require you to pay both black and green mana simultaneously. Therefore, tapping one swamp ({B}) and one forest ({G}) would pay the cost as {B/G}, not as separate black and green mana costs. 

Rule references:  
- 202.2d: "An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols, in addition to any other colors the object might be."  
- 107.4e: "A hybrid mana symbol such as {W/U} can be paid with either white or blue mana, and a monocolored hybrid symbol such as {2/B} can be paid with either one black mana or two mana of any type. A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors."
grounding_context:
202.1. A card’s mana cost is indicated by mana symbols near the top of the card. (See rule 107.4.) On most cards, these symbols are printed in the upper right corner. Some cards from the Future Sight set have alternate frames in which the mana symbols appear to the left of the illustration.
202.1a. The mana cost of an object represents what a player must spend from their mana pool to cast that card. Unless an object’s mana cost includes Phyrexian mana symbols (see rule 107.4f), paying that mana cost requires matching the type of any colored or colorless mana symbols as well as paying the generic mana indicated in the cost.
202.1b. Some objects have no mana cost. This normally includes all land cards, any other cards that have no mana symbols where their mana cost would appear, tokens (unless the effect that creates them specifies otherwise), and nontraditional Magic cards. Having no mana cost represents an unpayable cost (see rule 118.6). Note that lands are played without paying any costs (see rule 305, “Lands”).
202.2. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame.
202.2a. The five colors are white, blue, black, red, and green. The white mana symbol is represented by {W}, blue by {U}, black by {B}, red by {R}, and green by {G}.
Example: An object with a mana cost of {2}{W} is white, an object with a mana cost of {2} is colorless, and one with a mana cost of {2}{W}{B} is both white and black.
202.2b. Objects with no colored mana symbols in their mana costs are colorless.
202.2c. An object with two or more different colored mana symbols in its mana cost is each of the colors of those mana symbols. Most multicolored cards are printed with a gold frame, but this is not a requirement for a card to be multicolored.
202.2d. An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols and/or Phyrexian mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols, in addition to any other colors the object might be. (Most cards with hybrid mana symbols in their mana costs are printed in a two-tone frame. See rule 107.4e.)
202.2e. An object may have a color indicator printed to the left of the type line. That object is each color denoted by that color indicator. (See rule 204.)
202.2f. Effects may change an object’s color, give a color to a colorless object, or make a colored object become colorless; see rule 105.3.

Related rules:
107.4. The mana symbols are {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, {G}, and {C}; the numerical symbols {0}, {1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, and so on; the variable symbol {X}; the hybrid symbols {W/U}, {W/B}, {U/B}, {U/R}, {B/R}, {B/G}, {R/G}, {R/W}, {G/W}, and {G/U}; the monocolored hybrid symbols {2/W}, {2/U}, {2/B}, {2/R}, {2/G}, {C/W}, {C/U}, {C/B}, {C/R}, and {C/G}; the Phyrexian mana symbols {W/P}, {U/P}, {B/P}, {R/P}, and {G/P}; the hybrid Phyrexian symbols {W/U/P}, {W/B/P}, {U/B/P}, {U/R/P}, {B/R/P}, {B/G/P}, {R/G/P}, {R/W/P}, {G/W/P}, and {G/U/P}; and the snow mana symbol {S}.

Glossary:
- Card: The standard component of the game. Magic cards may be traditional or nontraditional. Tokens aren’t considered cards. In the text of spells or abilities, the term “card” is used only to refer to a card that’s not on the battlefield or on the stack, such as a creature card in a player’s hand. See rule 108, “Cards.”
- Cast: To take a card from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”
- Color: 1. A characteristic of an object. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.” 2. An attribute mana may have. See rule 106, “Mana.”
- Color Indicator: A characteristic of an object. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 204, “Color Indicator.”

105.1. There are five colors in the Magic game: white, blue, black, red, and green.
105.2. An object can be one or more of the five colors, or it can be no color at all. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame. An object’s color or colors may also be defined by a color indicator or a characteristic-defining ability. See rule 202.2.
105.2a. A monocolored object is exactly one of the five colors.
105.2b. A multicolored object is two or more of the five colors.
105.2c. A colorless object has no color.
105.3. Effects may change an object’s color or give a color to a colorless object. If an effect gives an object a new color, the new color replaces all previous colors the object had (unless the effect said the object became that color “in addition” to its other colors). Effects may also make a colored object become colorless.
105.4. If a player is asked to choose a color, they must choose one of the five colors. “Multicolored” is not a color. Neither is “colorless.”
105.5. If an effect refers to a color pair, it means exactly two of the five colors. There are ten color pairs: white and blue, white and black, blue and black, blue and red, black and red, black and green, red and green, red and white, green and white, and green and blue.

Related rules:
202.2. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame.

Glossary:
- Characteristic-Defining Ability: A kind of static ability that conveys information about an object’s characteristics that would normally be found elsewhere on that object (such as in its mana cost, type line, or power/toughness box). See rule 604.3.
- Color: 1. A characteristic of an object. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.” 2. An attribute mana may have. See rule 106, “Mana.”
- Color Indicator: A characteristic of an object. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 204, “Color Indicator.”
- Colorless: 1. An object with no color is colorless. Colorless is not a color. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.” 2. A type of mana. See rule 106, “Mana,” and rule 107.4c.

107.4a. There are five primary colored mana symbols: {W} is white, {U} blue, {B} black, {R} red, and {G} green. These symbols are used to represent colored mana, and also to represent colored mana in costs. Colored mana in costs can be paid only with the appropriate color of mana. See rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.”
107.4b. Numerical symbols (such as {1}) and variable symbols (such as {X}) represent generic mana in costs. Generic mana in costs can be paid with any type of mana. For more information about {X}, see rule 107.3.
107.4c. The colorless mana symbol {C} is used to represent one colorless mana, and also to represent a cost that can be paid only with one colorless mana.
107.4d. The symbol {0} represents zero mana and is used as a placeholder for a cost that can be paid with no resources. (See rule 118.5.)
107.4e. A hybrid mana symbol is also a colored mana symbol, even if one of its components is colorless. Each one represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways, as represented by the two halves of the symbol. A hybrid symbol such as {W/U} can be paid with either white or blue mana, and a monocolored hybrid symbol such as {2/B} can be paid with either one black mana or two mana of any type. A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors.
Example: {G/W}{G/W} can be paid by spending {G}{G}, {G}{W}, or {W}{W}.
107.4f. Phyrexian mana symbols are colored mana symbols: {W/P} is white, {U/P} is blue, {B/P} is black, {R/P} is red, and {G/P} is green. A Phyrexian mana symbol represents a cost that can be paid either with one mana of its color or by paying 2 life. There are also ten hybrid Phyrexian mana symbols. A hybrid Phyrexian mana symbol represents a cost that can be paid with one mana of either of its component colors or by paying 2 life. A hybrid Phyrexian mana symbol is both of its component colors.
Example: {W/P}{W/P} can be paid by spending {W}{W}, by spending {W} and paying 2 life, or by paying 4 life.
107.4g. In rules text, the Phyrexian symbol {H} with no colored background means any of the fifteen Phyrexian mana symbols.

Related rules:
107.3. Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X.
118.5. Some costs are represented by {0}, or are reduced to {0}. The action necessary for a player to pay such a cost is the player’s acknowledgment that they are paying it. Even though such a cost requires no resources, it’s not automatically paid.

Glossary:
- Background: An enchantment type that, in combination with the “choose a Background” ability, may allow a legendary enchantment card to be your commander. See rule 702.124, “Partner,” and rule 903, “Commander.”
- Color: 1. A characteristic of an object. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.” 2. An attribute mana may have. See rule 106, “Mana.”
- Colorless: 1. An object with no color is colorless. Colorless is not a color. See rule 105, “Colors,” and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.” 2. A type of mana. See rule 106, “Mana,” and rule 107.4c.
- Cost: An action or payment necessary to take another action or to stop another action from taking place. See rule 118, “Costs.”

question:
can you switch places in a team unified
i'm going to be playing my first team unified, my question is, if ive finished my round, as id be able to advise my teammates anyway, am i able to just take their place and play where they were playing?
answer:
The rules do not explicitly address switching places within a team during a Team Unified game. However, the rules for Team vs. Team (808) and Alternating Teams (811) variants do not mention the ability to switch seats during the game either. Since Team Unified is a variant of Team vs. Team, we can refer to rule 808.2, which states that "Each team sits together on one side of the table. Each team decides the order in which its players sit." This implies that once the seating is determined, players typically do not switch places during the game.

Therefore, based on the provided rules, there is no explicit rule allowing you to switch places with your teammates during a Team Unified game. You should check with your group to see if they have any house rules allowing for such a change.

Rule references: 808.2
grounding_context:
811.1. Alternating Teams games are played with two or more teams of equal size.
811.2. Any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins. The Alternating Teams variant uses the following default options.
811.2a. The recommended range of influence is 2. See rule 801, “Limited Range of Influence Option.”
811.2b. Exactly one of the attack left, attack right, and attack multiple players options must be used. See rule 803, “Attack Left and Attack Right Options,” and rule 802, “Attack Multiple Players Option.”
811.2c. The deploy creatures option isn’t normally used in the Alternating Teams variant.
811.3. At the start of the game, players are seated so that no one is next to a teammate and each team is equally spaced out.
Example: In an Alternating Teams game with three teams, A, B, and C, the seating around the table at the start of the game is A1, B1, C1, A2, B2, C2, A3, B3, C3, and so on.
811.4. A player can’t attack opponents who aren’t seated next to them, planeswalkers that aren’t controlled by opponents seated next to them, or battles that aren’t protected by opponents seated next to them.
811.5. In the Alternating Teams variant, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared. Teammates can’t review each other’s hands unless they are sitting next to each other. Teammates may discuss strategies at any time. Teammates can’t manipulate each other’s cards or permanents.

Glossary:
- Alternating Teams Variant: A multiplayer variant played among two or more teams of equal size. See rule 811, “Alternating Teams Variant.”
- Attack: To send a creature into combat offensively. A creature can attack a player or a planeswalker. See rule 508, “Declare Attackers Step.”
- Attack Multiple Players Option: An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants. See rule 802, “Attack Multiple Players Option.”
- Deploy Creatures Option: An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants to pass control of creatures between teammates. See rule 804, “Deploy Creatures Option.”
- Hand: 1. A zone. A player’s hand is where that player holds cards they have drawn but not played yet. 2. All the cards in a player’s hand. See rule 402, “Hand.”

808.1. Team vs. Team games are played with two or more teams. Each team may have any number of players on it.
808.2. Each team sits together on one side of the table. Each team decides the order in which its players sit.
808.3. Any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins. The Team vs. Team variant uses the following default options.
808.3a. The attack multiple players option is used (see rule 802).
808.3b. The deploy creatures options and limited range of influence options usually aren’t used in the Team vs. Team variant.
808.4. To determine which player goes first, randomly choose a team. If that team has an odd number of players, the player in its center seat goes first. If that team has an even number of players, the player to the left of its midpoint goes first. Turn order goes to the players’ left.
808.5. In the Team vs. Team variant, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared. Teammates may review each other’s hands and discuss strategies at any time. Teammates can’t manipulate each other’s cards or permanents.

Glossary:
- Attack Multiple Players Option: An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants. See rule 802, “Attack Multiple Players Option.”
- Hand: 1. A zone. A player’s hand is where that player holds cards they have drawn but not played yet. 2. All the cards in a player’s hand. See rule 402, “Hand.”
- Limited Range of Influence: An optional rule used in some multiplayer games that limits what a player can affect. See rule 801, “Limited Range of Influence Option.”
- Mana: The primary resource in the game. It is spent to pay costs, usually when casting spells and activating abilities. See rule 106, “Mana,” rule 107.4, and rule 202, “Mana Cost and Color.”

805.1. Some multiplayer games between teams use the shared team turns option. It’s always used in the Two-Headed Giant variant (see rule 810) and the Archenemy casual variant (see rule 904). It can be used only if the members of each team are sitting in adjacent seats.
805.2. Within each team, the player seated in the rightmost seat from that team’s perspective is the primary player. If the players on a team can’t agree on a choice, such as which creatures attack or what order triggered abilities are put on the stack, the primary player makes that choice.
805.3. The methods described in rule 103.1 are used to determine which team will take the first turn. The team determined this way is the starting team.
805.3a. The process for handling mulligans is altered accordingly. First, each player on the starting team, in whatever order that team likes, declares whether that player will take a mulligan. Then the players on each other team in turn order do the same. Teammates may consult while making their decisions. Then all mulligans are taken at the same time. Teammates may consult while choosing which cards, if any, to put on the bottom of their library. A player may take a mulligan even after a teammate has decided to keep their opening hand. See rule 103.5.
805.3b. The process for handling cards that allow a player to begin the game with them on the battlefield is altered accordingly. First, each player on the starting team, in whatever order that team likes, may put any or all such cards onto the battlefield from that player’s opening hand. Teammates may consult while making their decisions. Then each player on each other team in turn order does the same.
805.4. Each team takes turns rather than each player.
805.4a. The team whose turn it is is the active team. Each other team is a nonactive team.
805.4b. Each player on a team draws a card during that team’s draw step.
805.4c. Each player on a team may play a land during each of that team’s turns.
805.4d. An ability that triggers at the beginning of a step or phase may trigger multiple times if it triggers at the beginning of “each player’s” or “each opponent’s” step or phase. These abilities trigger once for each appropriate player if the ability’s trigger condition, effect, or intervening “if” clause refers to “that player,” “that opponent,” or similar.
805.5. Teams have priority, not individual players.

Related rules:
103.1. At the start of a game, the players determine which one of them will choose who takes the first turn. In the first game of a match (including a single-game match), the players may use any mutually agreeable method (flipping a coin, rolling dice, etc.) to do so. In a match of several games, the loser of the previous game chooses who takes the first turn. If the previous game was a draw, the player who made the choice in that game makes the choice in this game. The player chosen to take the first turn is the starting player. The game’s default turn order begins with the starting player and proceeds clockwise.

Glossary:
- Ability: 1. Text on an object that explains what that object does or can do. 2. An activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”
- Active Team: The team whose turn it is in a game using the shared team turns option. See rule 805.4a.
- Archenemy: 1. A casual variant in which a team of players faces off against a single opponent strengthened with powerful scheme cards. See rule 904, “Archenemy.” 2. A player in an Archenemy game who is playing with a scheme deck.
- Attack: To send a creature into combat offensively. A creature can attack a player or a planeswalker. See rule 508, “Declare Attackers Step.”

question:
Does Nim Deathmantle trigger in grave?
I had an opponent sac [[Nim Deathmantle]] with [[Krark-Clan Ironworks]], sac an artifact creature with Krark-Clan, and then trigger Nim Deathmantle from the graveyard.
Does this interaction hold up because Nim Deathmantle says "whenever a nontoken creature is put into your graveyard"?
answer:
Yes, Nim Deathmantle would trigger in this scenario. Nim Deathmantle's ability reads "Whenever a nontoken creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield, return that card to its owner's hand." Since Krark-Clan Ironworks causes a nontoken creature to be put into the graveyard, Nim Deathmantle's ability would trigger. 

The key rule here is 404.1, which states that any object that's countered, discarded, destroyed, or sacrificed is put on top of its owner's graveyard, and any instant or sorcery spell that's finished resolving is also put on top of its owner's graveyard. In this case, the artifact creature is being sacrificed, which puts it into the graveyard. 

The ability on Nim Deathmantle specifically triggers when a nontoken creature is put into the graveyard from the battlefield, which aligns with the scenario described. Therefore, Nim Deathmantle would indeed trigger and return to its owner's hand.
grounding_context:
404.1. A player’s graveyard is their discard pile. Any object that’s countered, discarded, destroyed, or sacrificed is put on top of its owner’s graveyard, as is any instant or sorcery spell that’s finished resolving. Each player’s graveyard starts out empty.
404.2. Each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile. A player can examine the cards in any graveyard at any time but normally can’t change their order. Additional rules applying to sanctioned tournaments may allow a player to change the order of cards in their graveyard.
404.3. If an effect or rule puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order.

- Discard: To move a card from its owner’s hand to that player’s graveyard. See rule 701.9, “Discard.”
- Effect: Something that happens in the game as a result of a spell or ability. See rule 609, “Effects.”
- Graveyard: 1. A zone. A player’s graveyard is their discard pile. 2. All the cards in a player’s graveyard. See rule 404, “Graveyard.”
- Instant: A card type. An instant is not a permanent. See rule 304, “Instants.”
- Object: An ability on the stack, a card, a copy of a card, an emblem, a token, a spell, or a permanent. See rule 109, “Objects.”
- Owner: The player who (for purposes of the game) a card, permanent, token, or spell belongs to. See rules 108.3, 110.2, 111.2, and 112.2.
- Pile: A temporary grouping of cards. See rule 700.3.
- Player: One of the people in the game. See rule 102, “Players.”

701.62a. “Manifest dread” means “Look at the top two cards of your library. Manifest one of them, then put the cards you looked at that were not manifested this way into your graveyard.” See rule 701.40, “Manifest.”
701.62b. An ability that triggers whenever a player manifests dread triggers after the process described in rule 701.62a is complete, even if some or all of those actions were impossible.
701.63. Endure
701.63a. Certain abilities instruct a permanent to endure N. To do so, that permanent’s controller creates an N/N white Spirit creature token unless they put N +1/+1 counters on that permanent.
701.63b. If a permanent is instructed to endure 0, nothing happens. No counters are put on that permanent and no tokens are created.

701.64a. “Harness [this permanent]” means “If this permanent isn’t harnessed, it becomes harnessed.”
701.64b. Harnessed is a designation that has no rules meaning other than to act as a marker that other spells and abilities can identify. Only permanents can be or become harnessed. Once a permanent becomes harnessed, it stays harnessed until it leaves the battlefield. Harnessed is neither an ability nor part of the permanent’s copiable values.
701.65. Airbend
701.65a. Certain spells and abilities instruct a player to airbend one or more permanents and/or spells. To do so, that player exiles those objects. For each card exiled this way, for as long as it remains exiled, its owner may cast it by paying {2} rather than paying its mana cost.
701.65b. An ability that triggers whenever a player airbends triggers when that player exiles one or more objects as a result of an instruction to airbend.
701.66. Earthbend
701.66a. “Earthbend N” means “Target land you control becomes a 0/0 land creature with haste in addition to its other types. Put N +1/+1 counters on it. When that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control.”
701.66b. An ability that triggers whenever a player earthbends triggers when the delayed triggered ability described in rule 701.66a is created.
701.67. Waterbend
701.67a. “Waterbend [cost]” means “Pay [cost]. For each generic mana in that cost, you may tap an untapped artifact or creature you control rather than pay that mana.”

701.40. Manifest

Glossary:
- Ability: 1. Text on an object that explains what that object does or can do. 2. An activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”

If I have a legendary land like \[\[Yavimaya, Cracle of Growth\]\], and somehow animate the land using \[\[Roaring Earth\]\], does it become a legendary creature? (for effects like \[\[Tyrite Sanctum\]\])

No, the land does not become a legendary creature when animated by Roaring Earth. The rules do not specify that animating a land with a creature ability changes its supertype or card type. Specifically, rule 205.4d only applies to permanents with the supertype "legendary" and does not cover the scenario of a land becoming a creature.

- 205.4: Supertypes like "legendary" are only explicitly applied to certain types of permanents (instant, sorcery, and legendary permanents).

The rules do not specify that copying Extraplanar Lens with Clever Impersonator or Mechanized Production would require exiling another land each time the copy enters the battlefield. This ability is a triggered ability that triggers when Extraplanar Lens enters the battlefield, and it applies to the original card and any copies of it. However, the rules do not state that this ability scales with the number of copies. Therefore, each copy of Extraplanar Lens will have its own instance of the ability, but it will not require exiling an additional land for each copy.

question:
Do spells cancel out other spells if it’s not explicitly stated?
For example let’s say my opponent plays a spell that says my creature does not untap until my opponents next turn, then on my turn let’s say I draw and can afford the mana cost of a spell that says I can untap my creature. Does my spell break theirs? Or does their spell have to play out?
answer:
The rules do not state that one spell automatically cancels out another. In the scenario described, the effect of your opponent's spell (702.95d) would continue to apply, causing your creature to not untap until their next turn. Your spell (which likely has an effect like "Untap target creature") would then allow you to untap the creature, but only after the effect of your opponent's spell has ended.

The key rule here is 614.0, which discusses the resolution of effects. Specifically, 614.0a states that when multiple simultaneous effects apply to the same object, the player has the option to choose the order in which the effects are applied. However, in this case, the effects are not simultaneous but sequential, with one effect preventing the untapping of the creature and another effect allowing it.

Therefore, your spell does not cancel out your opponent's spell; rather, it allows you to untap the creature after the effect of your opponent's spell has ended. The sequence of events would be:
1. Your opponent's spell prevents the creature from untapping until their next turn.
2. Your spell untaps the creature, but only after the effect of your opponent's spell has ended.

No specific rule explicitly states that one spell cancels another, so the effects are applied as described, with the second spell allowing the creature to untap after the first spell's effect has concluded.

question:
Can Verdabt Catacombs Search Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth?

On [[Verdant Catacombs]] it says to search your library for a swamp or forest card.
But on [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] it doesn't say anywhere that it is a swamp card. It only says that it is a legendary land and that it makes each land a swamp in addition to its other land types, but that isn't in effect when it's in the library anyway.

answer: No, Verdant Catacombs cannot search Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth from a player's library. According to rule 701.23b, when searching for cards with a specific quality, such as a "swamp" card, the player must find cards that match that quality. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth does not have the card type "swamp" or any card type at all when in a player's library. It only gains the "swamp" subtype when on the battlefield. Therefore, it would not be found by an instruction to search for a "swamp" card.

question:
Interaction between [[Hushbringer]], enchantment creatures and constellation triggers.
Lets say I have a \[\[Setessan Champion\]\] out. When an enchantment enters the battlefield I get to draw a card and the champion gets a +1/+1 counter. Would the same happen even if I also controlled a Hushbringer and the enchantment entering the battlefield was an enchantment creature (such as \[\[Alseid of Life's Bounty\]\])?
answer:
The interaction between [[Hushbringer]], [[Setessan Champion]], and constellation triggers would not change the outcome in this scenario. According to the rules, an Aura can't enchant an object or player outside its controller's range of influence (801.8). Since [[Hushbringer]] restricts the range of influence to 1, the constellation trigger on [[Setessan Champion]] would not trigger when an enchantment creature enters the battlefield because the entire event (the enchantment creature becoming a creature) happens outside [[Setessan Champion]]'s range of influence.

The relevant rule is:

801.7. A triggered ability doesn’t trigger unless its trigger event happens entirely within the range of influence of its source’s controller.
Example: In a game in which all players have range of influence 1, Alex is seated to the left of Rob. Rob controls two Auras attached to Alex’s Runeclaw Bear: One with the trigger condition “Whenever enchanted creature becomes blocked,” and one with the trigger condition “Whenever enchanted creature becomes blocked by a creature.” Alex’s Runeclaw Bear attacks the player to Alex’s left and becomes blocked. The ability of Rob’s first Aura triggers because the entire event (Runeclaw Bear becomes blocked) happens within Rob’s range of influence. The ability of Rob’s second Aura doesn’t trigger, however, because that event includes the blocking creature, which is out of Rob’s range.

The ability of Alex’s Extractor Demon doesn’t trigger because the leaves-the-battlefield event was outside Alex’s range of influence. question:
Interactions between Nissa, Who Shakes the World and cards like Yavimaya, Cradle of Growth and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove
I was wondering how Nissa, WSTH would interact with cards like dryad of the Ilysian Grove and yavimaya, Cradle of Growth? Since all my lands are technically forests, and the static ability says "when you tap a forest for mana add G", would I get an extra green, say, when I tap a swamp for B, or a Golgari Rot Farm for BG when Yavimaya is out?
answer:
The interaction you described would not work as intended. According to the rules, Nissa, Who Shakes the World's ability only applies to lands with the forest subtype, not to lands that could produce forest mana. Specifically:

- **509.1a** states that an effect that sets a land's subtype to one or more of the basic land types changes its land type. This means that if a land gains the forest subtype, it will have the forest land type and the associated forest mana ability.

- **305.7** explains that if an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, it loses its old land type and gains the appropriate mana ability for that new basic land type. However, this does not apply to lands that could produce forest mana but do not have the forest subtype.

- **305.9** clarifies that a land with the basic land type is a basic land, and a land that doesn't have the basic land type is a nonbasic land. Yavimaya, Cradle of Growth and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove are nonbasic lands, even though they could produce forest mana.

Therefore, when you tap a Swamp or a Golgari Rot Farm for black mana, you would not get an extra green mana because these lands do not have the forest subtype. Nissa, Who Shakes the World's ability only applies to lands that are actually forests, not to lands that could produce forest

question:
kindred dominance sudden substitution
P1 casts [[kindred dominance]]
P2 casts [[sudden substitution]]. Can P2 change the creature type of kindred dominance?
Thanks
answer:
No, P2 cannot change the creature type of [[Kindred Dominance]] with [[Sudden Substitution]]. 

The rules for Kindred cards (308.1) state that casting and resolving a kindred card follows the rules for casting and resolving a card of the other card type. Kindred Dominance is a kindred card, and its card type is not altered by its kindred nature. 

The effect of [[Sudden Substitution]] (511.1a) can change the card type of a permanent, but it specifically mentions that the permanent must be a creature. Kindred Dominance is not a creature, but an artifact (308.2). Therefore, [[Sudden Substitution]] cannot change the card type of Kindred Dominance.

question:
Luminous broodmoth vs archetype of imagination?
If i have a luminous broodmoth , and opponent has archetype of imagination how will Luminous broodmoth death triggers work. Ive seen several conflicting answers but narrow down to these 4
a) Creature that died will return to the battlefield without any flying counter as it cant have one given to it
b) Creature that died will return to the battlefield with a counter on it but still not be flying (will still trigger luminous broodmoth apon another death)
c) Creature that died will return to the battlefield with a counter on it but still not be flying (wont trigger Luminour broodmoth on death as has flying counter)
d) Creature that died will return to the battlefield with a counter on it and be flying as its not the creature itself hasnt gained flying just mearly has a flying counter attached to it?
answer:
The correct answer is:

d) Creature that died will return to the battlefield with a counter on it and be flying as its not the creature itself hasnt gained flying just mearly has a flying counter attached to it?

This is because the Luminous Broodmoth's afterlife ability creates Spirit creature tokens with flying. The key rule here is 702.135a, which states:

702.135a. Afterlife N means "When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, create N 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying."

The Spirit creature tokens created by the afterlife ability have flying, but it is a counter effect, not a characteristic of the token itself. Therefore, the token will have flying as long as the counter remains on it. The token will return to the battlefield with the flying counter, and it will be flying.

I assume it lives and would be able to uptick next turn
answer: No, the Planeswalker will not die from using its loyalty abilities. question:
Pact of Negation and Ritual Spells
If I cast [[Pact of Negation]] and when my turn comes around I only have 3 lands and no mana rocks on board can I save myself with a [[dark ritual]]?
answer: No, you cannot save yourself with a [[Dark Ritual]] in this scenario. According to the rules, you can only play one land per turn under normal circumstances (505.2). Additionally, [[Dark Ritual]] is a sorcery that requires you to pay 3 life and sacrifice a land to put two colorless artifact tokens onto the battlefield. Since you have only 3 lands and no mana rocks, you do not have enough lands to play a sorcery and do not meet the cost requirement for [[Dark Ritual]]. Therefore, you would not be able to use it to save yourself.

question:
Maestros Theater
Am I able to use [[Maestros Theater]] to search for [[Xander’s Lounge]] or just a basic land?
answer:
You can use [[Maestros Theater]] to search for either [[Xander’s Lounge]] or a basic land, but you are not required to find it if it is not in the specified zones. According to rule 701.23b, if a player is searching a hidden zone for cards with a stated quality, such as a card with a certain name or type, that player isn’t required to find some or all of those cards even if they’re present in that zone. 

In this case, Maestros Theater instructs you to search your library for a card with the name "Xander’s Lounge" or a basic land. Since you are searching for a specific named card or a basic land, you are not required to find it if it is not in your library. Therefore, you can choose to find zero, one, or two cards matching the criteria.
grounding_context:
701.23b. If a player is searching a hidden zone for cards with a stated quality, such as a card with a certain card type or color, that player isn’t required to find some or all of those cards even if they’re present in that zone.
Example: Splinter says “Exile target artifact. Search its controller’s graveyard, hand, and library for all cards with the same name as that artifact and exile them. Then that player shuffles their library.” A player casts Splinter targeting Howling Mine (an artifact). Howling Mine’s controller has another Howling Mine in her graveyard and two more in her library. Splinter’s controller must find the Howling Mine in the graveyard, but may choose to find zero, one, or two of the Howling Mines in the library.
701.23c. If a player is instructed to search a hidden zone for cards that match an undefined quality, that player may still search that zone but can’t find any cards.
Example: Lobotomy says “Target player reveals their hand, then you choose a card other than a basic land card from it. Search that player’s graveyard, hand, and library for all cards with the same name as the chosen card and exile them. Then that player shuffles their library.” If the target player has no cards in their hand when Lobotomy resolves, the player who cast Lobotomy searches the specified zones but doesn’t exile any cards.
701.23d. If a player is searching a hidden zone simply for a quantity of cards, such as “a card” or “three cards,” that player must find that many cards (or as many as possible, if the zone doesn’t contain enough cards).
701.23e. If the effect that contains the search instruction doesn’t also contain instructions to reveal the found card(s), then they’re not revealed.
701.23f. If searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Any abilities that trigger on a library being searched will trigger.
Example: Aven Mindcensor says, in part, “If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead.” Veteran Explorer says “When this creature dies, each player may search their library for up to two basic land cards, put them onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” An opponent who searched the top four cards of their library because of Veteran Explorer’s ability would shuffle the entire library.

question:
Can I reconfigure an enchantment?
I'm building a commander deck with [[Myrkul, Lord of Bones]] and I was wondering how it would interact with an equipment creature like [[Cloudsteel Kirin]]. After the cloudsteel dies would I be able to reconfigure the resulting enchantment onto another creature, or would it not work since it lost the equipment type?
answer: No, you would not be able to reconfigure the resulting enchantment onto another creature after the Cloudsteel Kirin dies. The Cloudsteel Kirin is an Equipment, and its reconfiguration ability (which is an ability that allows it to become an Aura enchantment) is tied to it being an Equipment. Once it dies and the enchantment enters the battlefield as an Aura, it no longer has the Equipment subtype. Therefore, it would not be able to be reconfigured onto another creature because the ability to reconfigure it as an Aura is no longer present on the card. The relevant rules are 301.5d and 301.5e, which discuss the separate controllership of Equipment and the conditions under which an Equipment enters the battlefield unattached.
grounding_context:
301.5d. An Equipment’s controller is separate from the equipped creature’s controller; the two need not be the same. Changing control of the creature doesn’t change control of the Equipment, and vice versa. Only the Equipment’s controller can activate its abilities. However, if the Equipment grants an ability to the equipped creature (with “gains” or “has”), the equipped creature’s controller is the only one who can activate that ability.
301.5e. If an effect attempts to put an Equipment that isn’t also an Aura (see rule 303.4i) onto the battlefield attached to either an object it can’t legally equip or an object that is undefined, the Equipment enters the battlefield unattached. If the Equipment is a token, it’s created and enters the battlefield unattached.
301.5f. An ability of a permanent that refers to the “equipped creature” refers to whatever creature that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isn’t an Equipment.
301.6. Some artifacts have the subtype “Fortification.” A Fortification can be attached to a land. It can’t legally be attached to an object that isn’t a land. Fortification’s analog to the equip keyword ability is the fortify keyword ability. question:
Cosima God of the Voyage, exiled and no land played?
So if you exile Cosima and then don't play a land, therefore not putting a Voyage Counter on Cosima, do you get to return Cosima to the battlefield during your main phase and treat X as 0?
answer:
No, you do not get to return Cosima to the battlefield during your main phase and treat X as 0. According to the rules, Cosima God of the Voyage can only be returned to the battlefield if a land is played, which would put a Voyage counter on her. If no land is played, she remains exiled and X remains 0. The rules do not provide a mechanism for returning an exiled Cosima to the battlefield without playing a land first.

Specifically, rule 701.11a states that "If Cosima is exiled, X is 0." Since Cosima is exiled and no land is played, X remains 0. There are no rules that allow for returning an exiled Cosima to the battlefield under these conditions.

question: If I get a 0/0 creature with [[Finale of Devastation]] with X>10, does it die immediately or does it get the +x/+x then die end of turn?
answer: The creature will get the +X/+X counter and then die at the end of the turn. According to rule 704.5g, a creature with toughness greater than 0 that has had lethal damage marked on it will die at the end of the turn if it has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked. Since the creature starts with 0 toughness and then gains +X/+X, it will have toughness greater than 0 at the end of the turn, and thus will not die immediately. The +X/+X will be applied, and the creature will die at the end of the turn due to having received lethal damage.

question:
Lazav the Multifarious and Cavern Harpy
Hey all,
I have a question about \[\[Lazav the Multifarious\]\] and \[\[Cavern Harpy\]\]. Several EDH lists for Lazav use Cavern Harpy as a way to return Lazav to hand in a pinch.
Here's what I don't understand about this: Cavern Harpy's ability specifically states "Return Cavern Harpy to its owners hand". Lazav's copy ability copies every detail of a card in your graveyard, but retains his name - the card is still called Lazav the Multifarious. So, if Lazav were to become a copy of Cavern Harpy and use his new activated ability, wouldn't the ability fizzle since it's looking specifically for a card named "Cavern Harpy", and there is no card with a such a name on the board?
answer:
The ability on Lazav the Multifarious would not fizzle because the rules for copying a card by name are different from the ability on Cavern Harpy. Specifically, rule 707.11 states:

707.11. If an effect refers to a permanent by name, the effect still tracks that permanent even if it changes names or becomes a copy of something else.

When Lazav the Multifarious copies Cavern Harpy, the copy will be Lazav the Multifarious, but it will have the ability "Return Lazav the Multifarious to its owner's hand." Even though Lazav the Multifarious is now a copy of Cavern Harpy, the ability is still referring to Lazav the Multifarious by name, not Cavern Harpy. Therefore, the ability will work as intended, returning Lazav the Multifarious to its owner's hand.

question:
Ashnod's Altar vs Phyrexian Altar
So when I sac a creature do I get one mana of any color and two colorless or do I have to choose between the two?
answer:
You have to choose between the two. Ashnod's Altar and Phyrexian Altar have different cost requirements:

- Ashnod's Altar (107.4f) allows you to pay {C}{C} or {0}{0} to sacrifice a creature and get two colorless mana.
- Phyrexian Altar (107.4f) allows you to pay {C}{C} or {0}{0} to sacrifice a creature and get one mana of any color plus two colorless mana.

The key difference is that Phyrexian Altar explicitly gives you one mana of any color, whereas Ashnod's Altar does not provide a color choice. Therefore, you must choose the color of the mana you receive when using Phyrexian Altar.

question:
Watcher in the Web with deathtouch dispute
Had a dispute last Friday over this. We had a group of five players playing with a lot going on. I was playing a spider deck and had Watcher in the Web (2/5 spider, can block up to 8 creatures) and a freshly cast Dragonlair Spider out. One players was threatened by my Dragonlair Spider and blitzed me with four 2/2 zombies and a flipped Quest for the Gravelord (5/5 zombie giant), overlooking the Watcher's abilities. Given the instants in my hand, I was jazzed!! The 5/5 led followed by the four 2/2's. I cast Giant Growth on the Watcher pumping it to 5/8 followed by Lace with Moonglove adding deathtouch to the mix. I declared the Watcher as the blocker and chose to do 1 damage to each zombie letting deathtouch work its magic. I saw it resolving with me losing the Watcher but destroying his entire assault. He claimed the 5/5 zombie giant and two 2/2 zombies would die but dealt lethal damage to the Watcher allowing the two remaining 2/2 zombies to live. question:
Creature gets/has ... for each ...
Hi fellow players,
I have some cards with the following text :"creature gets +1+1 for each land you control". Does this mean that, when the creature is on the battlefield and a new land is put on the battlefield, the creature gets an additional +1+1? Or does the 'gets'only apply once and the +1+1 remains the same?
I am confused because some other cards have text such as:"creature has...." instead of "creature gets....".
Can anyone explain? Many thanks in advance
answer:
The text "creature gets +1/+1 for each land you control" means that the creature will gain +1/+1 for each land that is on the battlefield at the time the ability resolves. This is a continuous effect that applies to the creature while it is on the battlefield. The effect is not locked in at the time the creature enters the battlefield but rather applies at the time the ability is resolved.

The key rule here is 611.2e, which states that if a resolving spell or ability both puts a nontoken permanent onto the battlefield and creates a continuous effect, that continuous effect applies simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. However, the continuous effect will then apply to the permanent at all times it is on the battlefield.

The use of "gets" in this context indicates that the effect is ongoing and will change based on the number of lands on the battlefield at the time the effect is applied. Therefore, if a new land is put on the battlefield, the creature will indeed gain an additional +1/+1.

The difference between "gets" and "has" is that "gets" typically refers to an effect that applies at a specific time, such as when a permanent enters the battlefield or when a spell resolves, while "has" can refer to a permanent characteristic that is always true as long as the permanent exists. However, in the context of the rules provided, both "gets" and "has" can be used to describe ongoing effects.

question:
Library of Leng with Lion’s Eye Diamond?
If I have LED and Library of Leng on the Battlefield and activate LED to discard my hand am I able to place some cards on top of my library? Is LED’s discard a cost or an effect? I’m not too clear on the interaction between the two cards.
Thanks for any help.
answer:
LED's ability to discard your hand is an additional cost to cast a spell or ability, not an effect that places cards on the bottom of your library. Therefore, it does not directly interact with Library of Leng, which allows you to put cards from the top of your library onto the bottom.

The relevant rules here are:
- **701.20d**: If cards in a player’s library are shuffled or otherwise reordered, any revealed cards that are reordered stop being revealed and become new objects. This rule does not apply since LED does not reorder your library.
- **701.20c**: A card that is currently revealed may be revealed again. This rule also does not apply since LED does not reveal cards.

The interaction between LED and Library of Leng is as follows:

question:
Quick, super-fast question about Aggravated Assault
During the "additional main phase" that Aggravated Assault gives me, can I drop a land? or....no?
Thanks everyone!
\please first roll your eyes first, and then respond to my noob Q. :)
answer: During the "additional main phase" that Aggravated Assault gives you, you can drop a land. According to rule 305.1, you may play a land card from your hand during a main phase when the stack is empty. Since Aggravated Assault creates an additional main phase, you can play a land during this phase as well.
grounding_context:
305.1. A player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Playing a land is a special action; it doesn’t use the stack (see rule 116). Rather, the player simply puts the land onto the battlefield. Since the land doesn’t go on the stack, it is never a spell, and players can’t respond to it with instants or activated abilities.
305.2. A player can normally play one land during their turn; however, continuous effects may increase this number.
305.2a. To determine whether a player can play a land, compare the number of lands the player can play this turn with the number of lands they have already played this turn (including lands played as special actions and lands played during the resolution of spells and abilities). If the number of lands the player can play is greater, the play is legal.
305.2b. A player can’t play a land, for any reason, if the number of lands the player can play this turn is equal to or less than the number of lands they have already played this turn. Ignore any part of an effect that instructs a player to do so.
305.3. A player can’t play a land, for any reason, if it isn’t their turn. Ignore any part of an effect that instructs a player to do so.
305.4. Effects may also allow players to “put” lands onto the battlefield. This isn’t the same as “playing a land” and doesn’t count as a land played during the current turn.
305.5. Land subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash. Land subtypes are also called land types. Lands may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3i for the complete list of land types.
Example: “Basic Land — Mountain” means the card is a land with the subtype Mountain.
305.6. The basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest. If an object uses the words “basic land type,” it’s referring to one of these subtypes. An object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability “{T}: Add [mana symbol],” even if the text box doesn’t actually contain that text or the object has no text box. For Plains, [mana symbol] is {W}; for Islands, {U}; for Swamps, {B}; for Mountains, {R}; and for Forests, {G}. See rule 107.4a. See also rule 605, “Mana Abilities.”

205.3i. Lands have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called land types. The land types are Cave, Desert, Forest, Gate, Island, Lair, Locus, Mine, Mountain, Plains, Planet, Power-Plant, Sphere, Swamp, Tower, Town, and Urza’s. Of that list, Forest, Island, Mountain, Plains, and Swamp are the basic land types. See rule 305.6.
107.4a. There are five primary colored mana symbols: {W} is white, {U} blue, {B} black, {R} red, and {G} green. These symbols are used to represent colored mana, and also to represent colored mana in costs. Colored mana in costs can be paid only with the appropriate color of mana. question:
Dragon's approach + burn triggers question
I have a question regarding an interaction. Do burn cards like [dragon's approach] deal burn damage to each opponent simultaneously or seperately?
To clarify: the first line of text on dragon's approach says: 'dragon's approach deals 3 damage to each opponent'. However does that mean that each opponent is dealt that damage at the same time or is each opponent being burned a seperate instance of damage?
The reason i'm asking is that there are cards that trigger off of damage being dealt. One example is [Chandra's spitfire]. It says: "Whenever an opponent is dealt noncombat damage, Chandra's Spitfire gets +3/+0".
Say I had a copy of Spitfire on the battlefield and I cast a copy of dragon's approach, would the spitfire trigger once for each opponent being burned or only once in total if the burn happens all at once?
answer:
The damage dealt by Dragon's Approach is processed as a single event, not multiple separate events. Specifically, the rules state:

120.4a. First, if an effect that’s causing damage to be dealt to a permanent states that excess damage that would be dealt to a permanent is dealt to another permanent or player instead, the damage event is modified accordingly. If the first permanent is a creature, the excess damage is the amount of damage in excess of what would be lethal damage, taking into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other sources that would be dealt at the same time. (See rule 120.6.)

This indicates that the damage is processed as a single event. Therefore, the damage dealt by Dragon's Approach to each opponent is processed as a single event, not multiple separate events.

120.4b. Second, damage is dealt, as modified by replacement and prevention effects that interact with damage. (See rule 614, “Replacement Effects,” and rule 615, “Prevention Effects.”) Abilities that trigger when damage is dealt trigger now and wait to be put on the stack.

Since the damage is processed as a single event, Chandra's Spitfire would trigger once for the total damage dealt by Dragon's Approach, not once for each opponent. Therefore, Chandra's Spitfire would trigger only once, gaining +3/+0 for each instance of damage dealt by Dragon's Approach.
grounding_context:

(See rule 120.6.) Any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch. (See rule 702.2.) If the first permanent is a planeswalker, the excess damage is the amount of damage in excess of that planeswalker’s loyalty, taking into account damage from other sources that would be dealt at the same time. question:
Lurrus
Can you play Lurrus as just a normal 3 drop in a deck? Or do you HAVE to only use him as a companion. Also when you cast spells from the graveyard using his ability where do they go? Or can he just continually cast the same spell from the graveyard?
answer:
Lurrus can be played as a normal 3-drop in a deck without using the companion ability. However, to use Lurrus's companion ability, you must follow the rules for revealing and using a companion card (702.139a-702.139d).

When you cast spells from the graveyard using Lurrus's ability, they are not put back into the graveyard. Instead, they are put onto the battlefield as mutated permanents (702.140c). You can continue to cast the same spell from the graveyard as many times as you can pay the cost, as long as the conditions for the companion ability are met and you have the necessary resources to pay the cost.
grounding_context:
702.139a. Companion is a keyword ability that functions outside the game. It’s written as “Companion—[Condition].” Before the game begins, you may reveal one card you own from outside the game with a companion ability whose condition is fulfilled by your starting deck. (See rule 103.2b.) Once during the game, any time you have priority and the stack is empty, but only during a main phase of your turn, you may pay {3} and put that card into your hand. This is a special action that doesn’t use the stack (see rule 116.2g). This is a change from previous rules.
702.139b. If a companion ability refers to your starting deck, it refers to your deck after you’ve set aside any sideboard cards. In a Commander game, this is also before you’ve set aside your commander.
702.139c. Once you take the special action and put the card with companion into your hand, it remains in the game until the game ends.
702.139d. Cards can enter Commander games from outside the game via the companion special action.

702.140a. Mutate appears on some creature cards. It represents a static ability that functions while the spell with mutate is on the stack. “Mutate [cost]” means “You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell’s mana cost. If you do, it becomes a mutating creature spell and targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as this spell.” Casting a spell using its mutate ability follows the rules for paying alternative costs (see 601.2b and 601.2f–h).
702.140b. As a mutating creature spell begins resolving, if its target is illegal, it ceases to be a mutating creature spell and continues resolving as a creature spell and will be put onto the battlefield under the control of the spell’s controller.
702.140c. As a mutating creature spell resolves, if its target is legal, it doesn’t enter the battlefield. Rather, it merges with the target creature and becomes one object represented by more than one card or token (see rule 730, “Merging with Permanents”). The spell’s controller chooses whether the spell is put on top of the creature or on the bottom. The resulting permanent is a mutated permanent.

question:
Magar of the Magic Strings
I have two questions with this [[Magar of the Magic Strings]].
1. What color are the creatures he makes? Are they colorless, since no color is specified, or are they of the color of the card being turned into a creature?
2. If someone were to exile one of the instant/sorcery creatures with something like [[Oblivion Ring]] and that Oblivion Ring were later removed, does the exiled "creature" come back?
answer:
1. The creatures Magar of the Magic Strings creates are of the color of the card being turned into a creature. Specifically, the color of the card being turned into a creature determines the color of the creature token created. This is because the card being turned into a creature does not have a mana cost or color indicator, and thus the color is determined by the card itself. Refer to rule 105.2, which states that an object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, and rule 202.2, which states that an object with no colored mana symbols in its mana cost is colorless. Since the card being turned into a creature does not have a mana cost, the color of the creature token is determined by the card itself.

2. The exiled "creature" would not come back if Oblivion Ring were removed. Oblivion Ring exiles the card, and when it is removed, the card returns to the zone it was exiled from, which is the exile zone. The card does not return to the battlefield or to the stack, so it does not come back as a creature. The effect of Oblivion Ring is to exile the card, and removing Oblivion Ring does not reverse the exile effect. Refer to rule 701.13, which describes the effect of Oblivion Ring.

question:
Confusion over Witness Protection
Hi everyone.
I just used Witness protection to enchant an opposing players creature. "Enchanted creature loses all abilities and is a green and white citizen creature with a base power and toughness of 1/1 named Legitimate Businessperson"
My opponent said if the legitimate businessperson dies his creature stays on the battlefield. I think it goes to the graveyard.
What is everyone's take on this?
answer:
The creature enchanted by Witness Protection will go to the graveyard if it dies. Witness Protection gives the enchanted creature protection from a quality, which means that any permanent with the specified quality that is already attached to the creature will not be put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. However, this does not apply to the creature itself. 

The relevant rules are:
- 702.16p: One Aura (Benevolent Blessing) gives the enchanted creature protection from a quality and says the effect doesn’t remove certain permanents that are "already attached to" that creature. This means that any objects with the stated quality that are already attached to that creature (including the Aura giving that creature protection) will not be put into their owners’ graveyards as a state-based action.
- 303.4e: The Aura’s controller is separate from the enchanted object’s controller or the enchanted player; the two need not be the same. If an Aura enchants an object, changing control of the object doesn’t change control of the Aura, and vice versa. Only the Aura’s controller can activate its abilities.

In this case, Witness Protection is an Aura that gives the creature protection from a quality, but it does not prevent the creature itself from being put into its owner's graveyard when it dies. Therefore, when the creature dies, it will go to the graveyard.
grounding_context:
702.16j. “Protection from everything” is a variant of the protection ability. A permanent or player with protection from everything has protection from each object regardless of that object’s characteristic values. Such a permanent or player can’t be targeted by spells or abilities and can’t be enchanted by Auras. Such a permanent can’t be equipped by Equipment, fortified by Fortifications, or blocked by creatures. All damage that would be dealt to such a permanent or player is prevented.
702.16k. “Protection from [a player]” is a variant of the protection ability. A permanent or player with protection from a specific player has protection from each object that player controls and protection from each object that player owns not controlled by another player, regardless of that object’s characteristic values. Such a permanent or player can’t be targeted by spells or abilities the specified player controls and can’t be enchanted by Auras that player controls. Such a permanent can’t be equipped by Equipment that player controls, fortified by Fortifications that player controls, or blocked by creatures that player controls. All damage that would be dealt to such a permanent or player by sources controlled by the specified player or owned by that player but not controlled by another player is prevented.
702.16m. Multiple instances of protection from the same quality on the same permanent or player are redundant.
702.16n. Some Auras both give the enchanted creature protection from a quality and say “this effect doesn’t remove” either that specific Aura or all Auras. This means that the specified Auras aren’t put into their owners’ graveyards as a state-based action. If the creature has other instances of protection from the same quality, those instances affect Auras as normal.

question:
Ground seal + osgir, the reconstructor
A while ago I played ground seal against an opponent that had osgir on the battlefield. I assumed it would help, but it seems that osgir does not mention 'target' anywhere in it's text, so it does not work.
While I accepted this as the correct answer, because I think it is, I find it a bit counterintuitive, since it is after all picking 1 specific card. Is this an opinion anyone else shares, or should I just get over it? With what I know of the rules so far, everything usually seems to make sense, so I'm hoping to hear something that can help me make sense to this too.
answer:
The Ground Seal you played does not work with Osgir, the Reconstructor because Osgir's ability does not have the word "target" in its text. Specifically, Osgir's ability reads:

"Osgir, the Reconstructor can't be the target of spells or abilities."

This means that Osgir cannot be targeted by spells or abilities, but it does not prevent you from targeting Osgir with Ground Seal. The key rule here is:

- **509.1a**: A spell or ability’s target must be legal when the spell or ability is cast and every time its effect resolves. A target that’s no longer in the zone it was in when the spell or ability was cast, that no longer has the characteristics specified for the target, or that’s no longer legal for some other reason, ceases to be a legal target.

In this case, Osgir can be the target of Ground Seal, but Ground Seal will have no effect because Osgir cannot be targeted by spells or abilities.

This might seem counterintuitive because it feels like Osgir should prevent targeting, but the rules are clear that the absence of "target" means it cannot be targeted, not that it prevents targeting. The rules are consistent, but sometimes the wording can be misleading.

To make it clearer, you can think of it this way:
- **Osgir** cannot be the target of any spell or ability.
- **Ground Seal**

question:
What happens when [[Shimmer]] leaves play?
As an example, let's say that I'm playing a commander game with 3 opponents, who each control 5 forests and I control 5 islands. I play Shimmer on my turn, name "forest", and wait for my next turn. Each of my opponents have their lands phase out. If I choose to sacrifice Shimmer, will my opponents lands phase back in and then lose phasing, or will they remain phased out for the rest of the game? If the latter is true and I somehow return Shimmer to the battlefield at a later point in the game, will my opponents lands gain phasing and then phase back in, or will they be unable to be affected by Shimmer because they are phased out? Thank you.
answer:
When [[Shimmer]] leaves play, any permanents that are phased out due to the phasing effect of Shimmer will remain phased out for the rest of the game. Specifically, the permanents phased out by Shimmer will not phase back in if [[Shimmer]] is removed from the game.

The key rules that apply here are:

- **702.26b**: "Except for rules and effects that specifically mention phased-out permanents, a phased-out permanent is treated as though it does not exist. It can’t affect or be affected by anything else in the game. A permanent that phases out is removed from combat." This means that once a permanent phases out, it remains phased out unless an effect specifically brings it back.

answer:
The rules do not specify the order in which you must cast the cards you exile with Jeska's Will. This process is repeated for each choice and decision needed to determine how an effect will operate.

Given these rules, you have the flexibility to cast Jeska's Will at any point in your turn, and you can choose to cast the exiled cards at any time you could cast an instant, including after you have already cast Jeska's Will.

Therefore, you do not have to cast the exiled cards as part of Jeska's Will's resolution. You can recast Jeska's Will and then cast the exiled cards at any time you choose, as long as you have the necessary mana and it is your main phase or an appropriate time to cast

question:
If a bounty counter from Mathas, Fiend Seeker is removed, can it be replaced by a bounty counter from a different source to trigger his ability?
I was looking at the text for [[Mathas, Fiend Seeker]] and noticed a potential neat interaction.
So, imagine this scenario:
 Player A has Mathas, Fiend Seeker and [[Bounty Hunter]] in play.

 Player B has [[Vampire Hexmage]] and [[Grizzly Bears]] in play.

 At the end of Player A's turn, they target Grizzly Bears with Mathas's triggered ability. Grizzly Bears gains a bounty counter and the ability “When this creature dies, each opponent draws a card and gains 2 life.” for as long as it keeps the counter.

 Then, Player A casts [Murder]] on Grizzly Bears.

 Player B responds by activating Vampire Hexmage's ability, targeting Grizzly Bears. It resolves, removing the bounty counter (and thus, the corresponding ability) from Grizzly Bears.

 Before Player A's Murder resolves, they activate their Bounty Hunter's first ability to put a new bounty counter on Grizzly Bears.

So here is my question: does Grizzly Bears regain the ability because it once again has a bounty counter on it?
answer: No, Grizzly Bears does not regain the ability because it once again has a bounty counter on it. The ability that Grizzly Bears gains when it has a bounty counter is a replacement effect that triggers when the creature dies, not a continuous effect that remains as long as the bounty counter is on the creature. According to rule 614.13, the effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield (in this case, the ability from Mathas, Fiend Seeker) may cause other objects to change zones. However, once the replacement effect has been applied and the ability has triggered, it is no longer in effect. The removal of the bounty counter by Vampire Hexmage's ability removes the trigger, and even if a new bounty counter is added, the trigger and the ability it creates do not reappear. Therefore, the ability does not return to Grizzly Bears.

question:
Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm Copy Questions
I have some copy questions please!
Scenario 1
I have \[\[Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm\]\] on the battlefield.
I cast \[\[Kilnmouth Dragon\]\]
I reveal 5 dragons, giving Kilnmouth 15 +1/+1 counters.
Question 1 - Copy only copies the cards text, not any added effects, so any counters added to the creature would not count?
Question 2 - In Kilnmouth case, assuming the counters are not copied, Amplify says "As this creatures enters the battlefield...", so could I reveal the 5 dragons again, and add 15 +1/+1 counters to the copy?
​
Scenario 2
I have Miiryum on the battlefield.
I also have \[\[Zirilan of the Claw\]\] on the battlefield, from my last turn.
I pay the cost, and tap Zirlian.
I search for a dragon, lets say \[\[BaleFire Dragon\]\]
Question 3 - Copy only copies the cards text, not any added effects, so the copy does not have haste?
Question 4 - The copy would not be exiled at my end step and stay on the battlefield after my turn ends, correct?
​
Thank you!
answer:
Scenario 1:
Question 1 - Yes, according to 707.4, any effects that add counters to the permanent do not get copied. The counters added by Kilnmouth Dragon are not copied to the Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm copy.

question:
Grist, the Hunger Tide as a commander + Umori as a companion?
Hi there. I decided on a whim to try and put together Insect/mill tribal with [[Grist, the Hunger Tide]] as the commander and with [[Umori, the Collector]] as a companion, however I'm unsure about something. The website that I'm using to build it, TappedOut, says my deck cannot have Umori as a companion, and at first I thought that was incorrect as I have 63 creatures and 36 lands, which equals 99 cards and meets the requirements for Umori, but I'm wondering if it has to do with Grist herself.
The ruling surrounding Grist that allows her to be a commander is as follows:
Grist, the Hunger Tide can be your commander as its first ability works before the game begins during deck construction.
The 'first ability' in this case refers to Grist's passive: As long as Grist, the Hunger Tide isn’t on the battlefield, it’s a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types.
The ruling regarding Companions in Commander is as follows:
You may have one companion in the Commander variant. Your deck, including your commander, must meet its companion requirement. Your companion is not one of your one hundred cards.
As far I can tell, Grist being treated as a creature when she's in the command zone is what allows her to be a commander in the first place, so that should also mean she fits the companion requirements that Umori asks of. Am I correct about this, or is there something I'm missing?
answer:
No, you are not correct about this. The key rule here is 903.3d, which states:

- If an effect refers to a characteristic of "your commander," it can find the appropriate player's commander and see its current characteristics, as modified by continuous effects and other rules, in all zones, including that player's library and hand.

While Grist, the Hunger Tide can be treated as a 1/1 Insect creature when in the command zone, this does not change the fact that she is still the commander card itself. The companion ability on Umori, the Collector, specifically refers to the card in your deck, not the characteristics of the commander in the command zone.

The companion ability on Umori, the Collector states:

- "Your deck, including your commander, must meet its companion requirement. Your companion is not one of your one hundred cards."

Since Grist, the Hunger Tide is the commander card and Umori, the Collector requires the entire deck, including the commander, to meet its companion requirement, Grist cannot be used as a companion.

Therefore, Umori, the Collector cannot be used as a companion with Grist, the Hunger Tide as the commander.

question:
Masked vandal vs path to exile
What happens when you exile masked as it enters the battlefield does the whole effect go off or no?
answer:
The effect of "Masked Vandal" going to the exile zone when it enters the battlefield does not trigger the full effect of "Path to Exile" because "Path to Exile" only exiles cards that are put into a graveyard from the library or hand. "Masked Vandal" is being exiled as it enters the battlefield, which is a different event. Therefore, "Path to Exile" does not apply to "Masked Vandal" in this scenario.

406.1. The exile zone is essentially a holding area for objects. Some spells and abilities exile an object without any way to return that object to another zone. Other spells and abilities exile an object only temporarily.
406.2. To exile an object is to put it into the exile zone from whatever zone it’s currently in. An exiled card is a card that’s been put into the exile zone.
406.3. Exiled cards are, by default, kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. Cards “exiled face down” can’t be examined by any player except when instructions allow it. However, if a player is instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or once a player is allowed to look at a card exiled face down, that player may continue to look at that card until it leaves the exile zone or is part of a pile of cards that are shuffled, even if the instruction allowing the player to do so no longer applies.
406.3a. A card exiled face down has no characteristics, but the spell or ability that exiled it may allow it to be played from exile. Unless that card is being cast face down (see rule 708.4), the card is turned face up just before the player announces that they are playing the card (see rule 601.2).
406.3b. Some spells and abilities allow a player to cast spells with certain qualities from among face-down cards in exile. A player may cast such a spell only if they are allowed to look at the face-down card in exile and if the resulting spell has the specified qualities.
406.4. Face-down cards in exile should be kept in separate piles based on when they were exiled and how they were exiled. If a player is instructed to choose an exiled card, the player may choose a specific face-down card only if the player is allowed to look at that card. Otherwise, they may choose a pile of face-down exiled cards, and then a card is chosen at random from within that pile. If choosing such a card is part of casting a spell or activating an ability, the chosen card isn’t revealed until after that cost is fully paid. (See rule 601.2i.)
406.5. Exiled cards that might return to the battlefield or any other zone should be kept in separate piles to keep track of their respective ways of returning. Exiled cards that may have an impact on the game due to their own abilities (such as cards with haunt) or the abilities of the cards that exiled them should likewise be kept in separate piles.

question:
Casting from graveyard
Just got the card "bramble worm" that has a 3-mana ability that goes "exile bramble worm from your graveyard: you gain 5 life". Would using this count as casting a spell from my graveyard? Thinking for the purpose of cards like ominous roost, and also the day-night cycle in innistrad.
Thanks in advance!
answer: No, using the ability on Bramble Worm would not count as casting a spell from your graveyard. The ability on Bramble Worm is an activated ability, not a spell. According to rule 702.138, an ability that reads "[This permanent] escapes with [one or more of a kind of counter]" or "[This permanent] escapes with [ability]" applies when the permanent escapes, which is defined in rule 702.138a as "If this permanent escaped, it enters with [those counters] or [that ability]." Since the ability on Bramble Worm does not fit this description, it does not escape or enter the battlefield in a way that would trigger effects for cards like Ominous Roost or the Day-Night Cycle in Innistrad.
