question:
Aegar, The Freezing Flame
Hello!
I was hoping someone would be able to answer a rules question for me.
Situation:
I have \[\[Niv-Mizzet, Parun\]\] and \[\[Aegar, the Freezing Flame\]\] out on the battlefield. My opponent has an indestructible creature out, lets say \[\[Stuffy Doll\]\]. Aegar says "Whenever a creature or planeswalker an opponent controls is dealt excess damage, if a Giant, Wizard, or spell you controlled dealt damage to it this turn, draw a card."
So Aegar doesn't even look to see if the creature died, just that its dealt excess damage. If Stuffy Doll, with 1 toughness, is dealt more than 1 damage, it would be excess, but since its indestructible, it does not die. In the same turn if I draw from Aegar, then use Niv-Mizzets triggered ability to deal another damage to stuffy doll, does that trigger Aegar's draw trigger again since stuffy doll at that point already has stacked lethal damage to it?
​
Thank you for any help :)
answer:
No, Aegar's trigger would not be triggered again in this scenario. According to rule 120.4a, when dealing damage, if an effect causes excess damage to be dealt to a permanent, the damage event is modified accordingly. In this case, the first damage to Stuffy Doll would be more than 1, making it excess damage. However, since Stuffy Doll is indestructible, it will not die, but the damage will still be applied.

When Niv-Mizzet's triggered ability deals additional damage to Stuffy Doll, it will again be more than 1, causing excess damage. However, because Stuffy Doll is already indestructible and has more than 1 damage, it will still not die. The key point is that Aegar's trigger condition is met only once per turn when the damage is first dealt, not each time additional damage is applied.

The relevant rule here is 120.4a, which states that if an effect causes excess damage to be dealt to a permanent, the damage event is modified accordingly. Since Stuffy Doll is indestructible, it will not die, but the excess damage will still be applied, triggering Aegar's ability once. Additional damage will not trigger Aegar's ability again because the condition of dealing excess damage has already been met.

question:

Can I use mana from [[Jeweled Lotus]] to mutate commanders onto a creature, like [[Vadrok, Apex of Thunder]] ?
answer: No, you cannot use mana from [[Jeweled Lotus]] to mutate commanders onto a creature like [[Vadrok, Apex of Thunder]]. The mutate cost is a fixed alternative cost that must be paid with the specified mana, and there is no rule that allows for additional mana to be used to pay this cost.

question:
Phyrexian Revoker Questions
Was playing a casual game of EDH and casted [[Phyrexian Revoker]], naming [[Yawgmoth, Thran Physician]], who was already on the board. Does Revoker’s effect use the stack like a ‘When’ ETB does? More directly, would the Yawg player have been able to remove Revoker via Yawg’s activated abilities in response to Revoker’s effect?
answer: No, Phyrexian Revoker's effect does not use the stack like a "When" triggered ability does. Specifically, the effect of Phyrexian Revoker that says "searches your library for a card with the same name as the card you removed, then puts that card into your hand" is an activated ability that is put onto the stack when the card is cast. According to rule 113.7a, once an ability is activated, it exists on the stack independently of its source. Therefore, the Yawg player would not have been able to remove Revoker via Yawg's activated abilities in response to Revoker's effect because the effect is not a triggered ability that can be countered. The effect of Phyrexian Revoker is an activated ability, and it resolves before any responses can be made.

113.7a. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.
113.8. The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it. The controller of a triggered ability on the stack (other than a delayed triggered ability) is the player who controlled the ability’s source when it triggered, or, if it had no controller, the player who owned the ability’s source when it triggered. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f.
113.9. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, and therefore can’t be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Static abilities don’t use the stack and thus can’t be countered at all.
113.10. Effects can add or remove abilities of objects. An effect that adds an ability will state that the object “gains” or “has” that ability, or similar. An effect that removes an ability will state that the object “loses” that ability.
113.10a. An effect that adds an activated ability may include activation instructions for that ability. These instructions become part of the ability that’s added to the object.
113.10b. Effects that remove an ability remove all instances of it.
113.10c. If two or more effects add and remove the same ability, in general the most recent one prevails. See rule 613 for more information about the interaction of continuous effects.

answer:
No, you cannot cast [[Bring to Light]] with more colors than are in your commander's color identity. According to rule 903.5c, a card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck's commander. 

In your case, your commander has a color identity of blue and green. Therefore, any card you include in your deck must also have a color identity that includes only blue and green. Since [[Darksteel Ingot]] produces red mana, it cannot be used to produce red mana for [[Bring to Light]], which requires red mana. 

Additionally, the color identity of [[Bring to Light]] is red, which is not in your commander's color identity. Thus, you cannot cast [[Bring to Light]] with colors not present in your commander's color identity.

Additionally, rule 118.9d states, "If an alternative cost is being paid to cast a spell, any additional costs, cost increases, and cost reductions that affect that spell are applied to that alternative cost." This means that while Jet Medallion's effect can be used as an alternative cost, it does not change the original mana cost of Baleful Mastery.

So, the correct way to cast Baleful Mastery with Jet Medallion would be to use its second ability, which allows you to cast it by paying {1}{B} rather than its original mana cost of {2}{B}.

question:
Suspend - Opponent's Commander
If I cast [[suspend]] on my opponent's commander, do they have to option to send it back to the command zone? I'm guessing they do, since suspend is exiling it...
answer: No, the opponent does not have the option to send the commander back to the command zone. When you cast [[suspend]] on an opponent's commander, it exiles the card as part of the suspend effect. The rules for suspend (724.2) state that every object on the stack, including the object resolving, is exiled. Since the commander is being exiled, it does not return to the command zone. The relevant rule is 724.2b, which states "Exile every object on the stack, including the object that’s resolving."

question:
Tatyova & Seventh Land
Whenever a land enters the battlefield under your control, if you control seven or more lands
Does this trigger if you're playing your seventh land or only after that?
answer:
The trigger occurs when you control seven or more lands, not when you're playing your seventh land. The trigger condition is based on the number of lands you control at the time the new land enters the battlefield, not the order in which they were played. Therefore, the ability would trigger when you control your eighth land, for example, but not when you play your seventh land. 

Rule reference: 603.6c discusses when a permanent enters the battlefield and triggers abilities, but it does not specify the order of events. The condition is checked at the time the land enters, not when it is played.

question:
Using Koma to tap lands.
Was in a game of EDH today that came to a standstill for a few minutes due to no one completely knowing how to resolve this.

Opponent was playing Koma. Cosmos Serpent and was arguing that it's ability that taps permanents can target lands like Gaea's Cradle before I'm able to tap it for mana. I said that tapping Gaea's Cradle would give me the mana before Koma can tap it.
Could I please get some sort of ruling to verify this please?
answer:
The ruling you are looking for can be found in the following rules:

- **605.4a**: A triggered mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority.
- **601.2g**: If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid.

In your scenario, Koma Cosmos Serpent has an ability that allows it to tap permanents as a triggered ability. This ability is a triggered mana ability, which means it resolves immediately without waiting for priority. Therefore, when Koma taps a land like Gaea's Cradle, the mana from Gaea's Cradle would be available to be used to pay for the cost of Koma's ability.

The sequence of events would be:
1. Koma's ability triggers.
2. The triggered ability resolves, tapping the land.
3. The player has a chance to activate mana abilities, which would include using the mana from the tapped land to pay for Koma's ability.

So, you are correct that you can use the mana from Gaea's Cradle to pay for Koma's ability, as the mana is available before Koma can tap the land.

Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty and Apex Devastator
In this scenario I have [[Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty]] on the battlefield and then cast [[Apex Devastator]].
Does Imoti give Devastator a fifth cascade? Or does cascade trigger the normal number of times: four?
answer:
The cascade ability on Apex Devastator will trigger the normal number of times, which is four, regardless of the effects on the battlefield. question:
Casting a spell with an illegal target.
I think explains it well enough, but I want to ensure I understand it fully in case I need to argue my position.
If I try to cast a spell on a creature with Protection or Shroud and there are other legal targets on the board, which of the following occurs?
A. I rewind to before I cast the spell(return to hand, untap lands, etc) and can choose to cast again on a legal target, make targets legal then cast again, or not cast at all at my discretion.
B. The spell fizzles and goes to the GY, but triggered abilities on casting spells still apply(IE Magecraft).
C. Though my original target is illegal, as I started casting I have to choose a legal target, be it belonging to the same player, a different one, or another type of permanent.
I'm fairly certain it is A, but are there any nuances or cases where it wouldn't work like that?
Likely inconsequential to the actual question, some context to those curious/bored:
Last Friday I was playing commander at my LGS. I've been playing MTG for years but just started playing commander the past few months. Playing with some people I've never met before, the game was about to end and as a last-ditch effort I was trying to mill out someone with [[Consuming Aberration]] and cast [[Feed the Swarm]] on an opponent's 1cmc creature, not realizing they had an enchantment that shared [[White Knight]]'s protection from black with it. They pointed it out and said the spell fizzles and goes to the GY, but I still get the cast trigger. Since that's all I was looking for and the game ended the next turn I didn't argue, but that seemed wrong to me.
Next game I tried casting [[Chandra's Ignition]] on a 48/48 creature that had [[Lightning Greaves]] equipped, and the same player pointed out they were an illegal target. They also insisted that since I had another creature(with 1 power) I had to follow through with it as my only legal target. This also seemed wrong as it wasn't consistent with what occurred previously but the rest of the table seemed to take his side so I didn't try to argue back.
Traditionally I always had myself or the other player rewind when an illegal action occurred, though as I usually play casually or would be gracious whenever possible I didn't know if that was aligned with the actual rules or just a casual thing.
Thank you!
answer:
The correct answer is A. According to the rules, if a spell or ability has an illegal target, the spell or ability doesn't resolve, and it is removed from the stack. However, the game returns to the moment before the spell was cast, allowing you to choose a new target or take other actions as if the spell never happened.

Specifically, rules 601.6 and 608.2b cover this scenario:
- **601.6**: If a player is no longer allowed to cast a spell after completing its proposal, the casting of the spell is illegal, and the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed.
- **608.2b**: If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. If all targets are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn't resolve.

Therefore, you can choose to cast the spell again on a legal target, choose not to cast it, or take any other action as if the spell never happened.

The scenarios you described with [[Feed the Swarm]] and [[Chandra's Ignition]] are consistent with this rule. In both cases, the spell would be removed from the stack, and you would be able to choose a new target or not cast the spell at all.

If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects don’t apply to illegal targets. question:
Whip of Erebos and Conjurer’s Closet
If during my main phase I use [[Whip of Erebos]] to bring back x creature and I have [[Conjurer’s Closet]] on the board, when my end step occurs can I exile x creature to keep it on the board?
answer:
The rules do not explicitly allow or prohibit exiling a creature to keep it on the board during the end step. However, the end step is a state-based action check phase where certain conditions are checked and effects that trigger at the end of the turn are processed. Exiling a creature is not a state-based action, and it is not an effect that triggers at the end of the turn. Therefore, based on the provided rules, you cannot use the end step to exile a creature to keep it on the board.

The relevant rules for the end step are:
- 724.1b: Exile every object on the stack, including the object that’s resolving. All objects not on the battlefield or in the command zone that aren’t represented by cards will cease to exist the next time state-based actions are checked.
- 724.1c: Check state-based actions. No player gets priority, and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack.

Since exiling a creature is not a state-based action and does not trigger an ability, it cannot be done during the end step.

Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game.

question:
Crop Rotation + Kudzu?
If Kudzu is enchanting one of my Forests, can I tap said Forest for mana, pay for Crop Rotation which goes on the stack after the Kudzu destroy trigger, and still choose a new target for Kudzu even though Crop Rotation sacced the land before Kudzu could destroy it?
I don't see anything about Kudzu needing to destroy the land in order to give the player a choice to re-attach to a new land.
answer:
The rules do not specify that Kudzu must destroy the land before giving the player a choice to re-attach to a new land. According to the rules, Kudzu's ability allows the player to choose a new permanent to enchant after the destruction of the current permanent. 

The key part of the rules is in Kudzu's ability, which states:
- "Enchant land" - This means Kudzu can be attached to a land.
- "If that land is put into its owner's graveyard, you may choose a land you control and attach Kudzu to it" - This part allows the player to choose a new land to enchant Kudzu after the current land is destroyed.

Therefore, the sequence of events can be:
1. You tap the Forest to pay for Crop Rotation.
2. Crop Rotation resolves, sacrificing the Forest.
3. The Forest is put into its owner's graveyard.
4. You may choose a new land to attach Kudzu to.

The rules do not prevent you from choosing a new land after the current one is destroyed. The choice to re-attach Kudzu to a new land is given after the destruction, not before.

Rule references:
- 616.1 - For the process of choosing which effect to apply when multiple effects modify an event.
- 701.68 - For the specifics of Kudzu's ability.
grounding_context:
616.1. If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4).
616.1a. If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects are self-replacement effects (see rule 614.15), one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1b.
616.1b. If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would modify under whose control an object would enter the battlefield, one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1c.
616.1c. If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would cause an object to become a copy of another object as it enters the battlefield, one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1d.
616.1d. If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would cause a card to enter the battlefield with its back face up, one of them must be chosen (See rule 701.27, “Transform,” and rule 701.28, “Convert.”). If not, proceed to 616.1e.
616.1e. Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen.
616.1f. Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply.
Example: Two permanents are on the battlefield. One is an enchantment that reads “If a card would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it,” and the other is a creature that reads “If this creature would die, instead shuffle it into its owner’s library.” If the creature is destroyed, its controller decides which replacement to apply first; the other does nothing.

question:
Gloomshrieker + Mutate
if \[Gloomshrieker\] is mutated on bottom, and it dies, does it still get exiled? because it's names changed
answer: Yes, Gloomshrieker still gets exiled when it dies, even though its name has changed. The key rule here is 712.21c, which states that if an effect can find the new object that a melded permanent becomes as it leaves the battlefield, it finds both cards. Since Gloomshrieker is a melded permanent, when it dies, the effect that exiles it will find both cards (Midnight Scavengers and Graf Rats) and exile them. The change in its name does not affect the exiling process.

The rules do not provide specific information on how to handle the scenario where a player activates an ability in response to another player casting a spell. However, based on the rules provided, we can infer the following:

1. When Player B casts a spell, it goes on the stack. Player A can respond by activating an ability, which also goes on the stack.

Since Player A activates an ability in response to Player B casting a spell, Player A's ability will be placed on the stack after Player B's spell. The stack will then be resolved from the top down.

question:
Trouble with a hydra
I use this combo which works pretty well. I build a boardstate with creatures and then I drop Finale of devastation pumped for ten or more. The card I pull is Kalonian Hydra. On attack this card doubles the number of +1/+1 counters on all creatures. So a seemingly weak boardstate can quickly become threat number one.
My question is about after the turn ends. Would the doubled counters on the creatures stay or be shed. I know the initial amount would shed, but what about the additional that are applied through the Hydra?
answer:
The additional +1/+1 counters added by Kalonian Hydra would stay on the creatures even after the turn ends. According to rule 704.8, state-based actions are performed at the end of a player's turn to determine if a permanent has left the battlefield. Since the +1/+1 counters are applied as part of the state of the game, they are not removed by state-based actions.

Specifically, the +1/+1 counters are applied as part of the game state when Kalonian Hydra's ability resolves. These counters are not counters that are placed or removed by a player's action, but rather part of the permanent's state. Therefore, they remain on the creatures even after the turn ends.

I target an opponent's permanent with [[Wild Magic Surge]] and the permanent becomes indestructible.
Does the remainder of Wild Magic Surge resolve, grabbing a permanent of the same type out of the opponent's deck and putting it into play?
The card doesn't seem to have an "if" clause, the wording doesn't imply the destruction of the target is required for it to resolve.
answer:
Yes, the remainder of Wild Magic Surge will resolve. According to the rules provided, since Wild Magic Surge does not have an "if" clause, it will continue to resolve as written. The target becoming indestructible does not prevent the rest of the spell from resolving because there is no condition that requires the target to be destroyed for the spell to continue resolving.

Specifically, rule 608.2m states that if an instant spell or ability that can legally resolve leaves the stack once it starts to resolve, it will continue to resolve fully. Since Wild Magic Surge is an instant spell and does not have an "if" clause that would be modified by the target becoming indestructible, it will resolve as intended, drawing a card and putting a permanent onto the battlefield.

question:
Zedruu, the Greathearted and Wedding Ring
Does the token created by wedding ring for the opponent count as a permanent I own under my opponent's control for the purpose of triggering Zedruu's ability? Thanks in advance!
answer:
No, the token created by the Wedding Ring does not count as a permanent you own under your opponent's control. The relevant rules are:

- Rule 109.4g: "In a Conspiracy Draft game, each conspiracy card is controlled by its owner." This establishes that the controller of a conspiracy card is its owner.
- Rule 109.5: "The words ‘you’ and ‘your’ on an object refer to the object’s controller, its would-be controller (if a player is attempting to play, cast, or activate it), or its owner (if it has no controller)." This clarifies that for a triggered ability, "you" refers to the controller of the object when the ability triggered.

In this case, Zedruu, the Greathearted's ability triggers when a player controls a creature with the Ring-bearer designation. The token created by the Wedding Ring is controlled by the player who owns the card, not by the player whose turn it is or who controls Zedruu. Therefore, the token does not count as a permanent you own under your opponent's control.

question:
Undying Evil
The card Undying Evil has no rulings on gatherer, but I am confused as to how it works. It gives a creature undying, but does it still have undying upon returning to the battlefield, or does undying finish its effect and wear off? I am asking because I want to be able to use it with Ghave, Guru of Spores to help as a combo piece if it is possible to do so.
answer:
According to the rules, when a permanent with undying leaves the battlefield, the undying ability triggers and checks if the permanent had any +1/+1 counters on it. If it did not have any +1/+1 counters, the undying ability returns the permanent to the battlefield under its owner's control with a +1/+1 counter on it. However, once the permanent returns to the battlefield, the undying ability finishes its effect, and the permanent no longer has undying.

Specifically, this is governed by rule 702.93a:

702.93a. Undying is a triggered ability. “Undying” means “When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner’s control with a +1/+1 counter on it.”

The key phrase here is "When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield," which means the undying ability only triggers when the permanent is being put into the graveyard. Once the permanent returns to the battlefield, the undying ability has already finished its effect, and the permanent no longer has undying. Therefore, you cannot use Undying Evil to return a creature with undying to the battlefield to reuse its undying ability.

Before state-based actions are performed, Young Wolf has one +1/+1 counter and three -1/-1 counters on it. After state-based actions are performed, Young Wolf is in the graveyard. When it was last on the battlefield, it had a +1/+1 counter on it, so undying will not trigger.

question:

If I reanimate [[Vilis, Broker of Blood]], does the life loss from [[Reanimate]] trigger Vilis’ card draw ability?
answer: No, the life loss from Reanimate does not trigger Vilis, Broker of Blood's card draw ability. Vilis's ability is triggered by the beginning of a player's precombat main phase, not by life loss. The life loss from Reanimate is a consequence of the triggered ability associated with rad counters, as described in 728.1a. Vilis's ability is an inherent triggered ability that checks for the presence of rad counters at the beginning of a player's precombat main phase, not for life loss. Therefore, the life loss does not meet the condition to trigger Vilis's ability.

question:
Harmonic Prodigy and Mana Abilities
I was looking at some potential combos with \[\[Harmonic Prodigy\]\] . I saw a card named \[\[Orochi Leafcaller\]\] an wondered if this combination would theoretically make infinite mana. The rulings I found say that mana abilities are triggered abilities therefore a mana ability would be seen and duplicated by the \[\[Harmonic Prodigy\]\] if I'm not mistaken. It seems like something that wouldn't work at all. I think there's a simple ruling I'm looking over, if you could help all comments would be appreciated.
answer:
The combination of Harmonic Prodigy and Orochi Leafcaller does not create an infinite mana loop. Here’s why:

1. **Orochi Leafcaller’s Ability**: Orochi Leafcaller has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any type of land an opponent controls could produce.” This is a triggered ability, but it is not a mana ability. According to rule 605.5, an ability with a target is not a mana ability, and a spell can never be a mana ability. Need help with ruling
If i blink Pendant of prosperity with Aminatou, the fateshifter's \[−1\]: Exile another target permanent you own, then return it to the battlefield under your control. under whose control does it enter?
answer:
The Pendant of Prosperity enters the battlefield under the controller who exiled it, which is the player who cast Aminatou, the Fateshifter. This is because the ability of Aminatou, the Fateshifter, specifically states that the permanent is returned to the battlefield under the controller's control. The relevant rule is:

608.2k. If an ability's effect refers to a specific untargeted object that has been previously referred to by that ability's cost or trigger condition, it still affects that object even if the object has changed characteristics.

In this case, the ability of Aminatou, the Fateshifter, refers to the permanent that was exiled, and thus the permanent returns to the battlefield under the controller's control who cast Aminatou, the Fateshifter.

question:
mdfcs in the other zones
So I'm under the impression that mdfcs only count as their front face in all zones other than battlefield, but arena lets me play the backside of agadeems awakening through ramunap excavator from my graveyard. Is this an arena problem or is that actually how it works? If so could I also, say, search up toralf with[[ forging the tyrite sword]] since his back is an equipment?
answer:
This is an arena problem. According to the rules, a double-faced card (mdfc) put onto the battlefield from any zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default (712.14). If a spell or ability puts an mdfc onto the battlefield transformed or converted, it enters the battlefield with its back face up (712.14a). However, Arena's behavior does not align with these rules.

For your specific examples:
- **Agadeem's Awakening**: Since its back face is a sorcery, it would be put into the graveyard if played from the graveyard, as per 712.13a.
- **Toralf, Bartered Blade**: Since his back face is an equipment, it would also be put into the graveyard if played from the graveyard, as per 712.13a.

Therefore, Arena's behavior is not in line with the official rules.

question:
Question about damage triggers and death
I have kind of a stupid question about Dragonborn champion, who lets me draw a card whenever a source of mine deals 5 damage to a player.
Let's say i attack with him and another 5 power creature. In the damage assignment step Dragonborn champion gets blocked to death by my opponent, the other creature swings for 5 damage in my opponents face. Damage is dealt simultaniously, does that mean that Dragonborn champions ability triggers? Or does it not trigger, since he is basically dead when my other creature deals damge? Thanks in advance!
answer:
The Dragonborn champion's ability would not trigger in this scenario. Here's why:

1. **Simultaneous Damage Assignment**: According to rule 120.9, if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources, and the effect refers to "the damage dealt," it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources.

2. **Death Before Triggering**: The Dragonborn champion is blocked to death by the opponent, meaning it will be destroyed as a state-based action (see rule 120.5) before the other 5 damage is dealt. Since the champion is no longer a legal source of damage by the time the other creature deals its damage, the ability does not trigger.

Therefore, the ability "Draw a card whenever a source of mine deals 5 damage to a player" does not trigger because the Dragonborn champion is destroyed before the other creature deals its damage. The specific timing and sequence of events are crucial in determining whether an ability triggers.

question:
Neverwinter Hydra dice ruling
Neverwinter Hydra. X X GG Cost.
"As Neverwinter Hydra enters the battlefield, roll XD6. It enters with a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the total of those results"
If I Pay 1X 1X GG, Am I rolling 1 D6? or 2 D6 and adding together? That's a really low cost (4 Mana) for what COULD be 12/12. Or would it be more apt to be 2X 2X G G for a possibility of 12/12 with 2D6? No one online can seem to agree on this, and the description is incredibly open ended.
answer:
The ruling for how many dice to roll is based on the cost and the text of the card. According to the rules provided:

- The card states "roll XD6" where X is the number of X in the cost. (509.1a)
- In this case, the cost is 1X 1X GG, which means X is 1. Therefore, you should roll 1D6. (509.1a)

The rule 706.3c does not apply here because it pertains to effects that include "Roll again," which is not present in the card's text. The number of dice to roll is directly specified by the cost and the card's text.

So, you would roll 1D6, not 2D6. The card's text does not imply that you should roll multiple dice and add them together; it simply states to roll the number of dice indicated by the X in the cost.

question:
Regeneration can you do it twice?
Answered
So someone plays a card targeting my skeleton(or anything with reg) and I choose to regenerate it, before it gets to my turn they play another spell targeting it to destroy it. Can I regenerate it twice before my turn?
I read somewhere to have something reg it needs to tap?
answer:
No, you cannot regenerate the same permanent twice with the same regeneration effect. According to rule 614.6, if an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. In this case, the first regeneration effect would replace the destruction event, causing the permanent to be tapped and removing all damage. If another destruction event occurs before your turn, the second regeneration effect would again replace the destruction event, causing the permanent to be tapped and removing all damage. However, once the permanent is tapped due to the first regeneration effect, it cannot be regenerated again by the same effect because the destruction event has been replaced and the permanent is no longer being destroyed.

The key rule here is 614.6, which states: "If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities." This means that once the permanent is tapped due to the first regeneration effect, the destruction event is replaced and the permanent is no longer being destroyed, so the second regeneration effect would not trigger.

question:
Follow up question regarding Astral Slide and removal
So it seems like you all agree that you can cycle and trigger Astral Slide/Drift's ability in response to targeted removal but I still have some confusion. Wouldn't the cycling have to resolve first for the Astral Slide ability to trigger thus making the previously stated scenario not possible? Am I missing something or just not understanding how the stack works here?
answer:
The key point here is understanding the timing and the stack. When a card with Astral Slide is targeted by removal, you can respond by cycling the card to trigger its ability. The cycling action resolves before the removal spell resolves, allowing the ability to trigger.

Here’s the relevant sequence of events:

1. The removal spell is cast, targeting the Astral Slide.
2. You respond by cycling the Astral Slide.
3. The cycling action resolves, triggering the ability.
4. The ability is now on the stack.
5. The removal spell resolves, destroying the Astral Slide.
6. The ability resolves, causing the Astral Slide to drift to a random player.

The crucial rule here is 603.2, which describes how triggered abilities are created:

- 603.2a. When a game event or game state meets the trigger event, the ability becomes activated, and its controller gets priority to activate it or allow it to resolve.

In this case, the cycling action resolves, and the ability to trigger is created. The removal spell then resolves, destroying the Astral Slide, but the ability to trigger has already been created and is on the stack. Therefore, the ability to drift to a random player will resolve after the removal spell has resolved.

The stack works such that the cycling action resolves first, creating the triggered ability, which then goes on the stack. The removal spell resolves after, but the triggered ability still resolves afterward.

question:
Tergrid unanswered?
if two players have tergrid god of fright and a third discards/sacs, who gets the trigger?
answer:
The rules do not explicitly cover the scenario where two players have Tergrid, God of Fright and a third player discards or sacrifices a card. However, we can infer the resolution based on the rules provided.

The relevant rule here is 701.21, which describes the sacrifice action. When a player sacrifices a card, it is done directly to their graveyard, and it doesn't directly affect the trigger of Tergrid, God of Fright.

Tergrid, God of Fright has the following ability:
- 701.21a. To sacrifice a permanent, its controller moves it from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard.

The trigger for Tergrid, God of Fright is:
- 701.21a. "Whenever a player sacrifices a creature, Tergrid, God of Fright gets +1/+1 until end of turn."

Since the sacrifice action is performed by a player, and the trigger is based on a player sacrificing a creature, the trigger will be for the player who performed the sacrifice.

Therefore, if a third player discards or sacrifices a card, the trigger will be for the player who performed the discard or sacrifice, not for the players with Tergrid, God of Fright.

No specific rule number directly addresses this scenario, but the logic follows from the sacrifice and trigger rules provided.

question:
Beginning of upkeep triggers
Tried looking at all the rulings and i cant find info if cards entering the beginning of upkeep can also get beginning of upkeep triggers that turn. An example would be if "Braids, Conjurer Adept" brings in "Gate to the Aether" onto the battlefield, would "Gate to the Aether" be able to trigger that same turn?
answer:
According to the provided rules text, when a permanent with an ability that triggers "at the beginning of the upkeep" enters the battlefield during the upkeep step, that ability won't trigger until the next turn's upkeep step. This is because the upkeep step doesn't "back up" to allow those abilities to go on the stack.

Specifically, rule 503.1a states:
"Any abilities that triggered during the untap step and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesn’t matter."

And rule 503.2 clarifies:
"If a permanent with an ability that triggers 'at the beginning of the upkeep' enters the battlefield during this step, that ability won’t trigger until the next turn’s upkeep step. Likewise, if a delayed triggered ability that triggers 'at the beginning of the next upkeep' is created during this step, that ability won’t trigger until the next turn’s upkeep step."

Therefore, in the example given, if "Braids, Conjurer Adept" brings "Gate to the Aether" onto the battlefield during the upkeep step, "Gate to the Aether" will not trigger its "at the beginning of the upkeep" ability that turn. It will trigger at the beginning of the next upkeep step.

[[Planar Void]] triggers for each card individually and maybe therefore also triggers [[Tormod, the Desecrator]] 5 times?

question:
Raised by Giants and the Command Zone
If I have Raised by Giants as my background and my commander is in the command zone, is he a giant? Or do I need to have both on the battlefield in order for the background’s ability to be present?
answer:
The background Raised by Giants does not affect permanents in the command zone. The ability "If a legendary creature card is in the command zone, that card becomes a giant creature card" only applies to legendary creature cards that are in the command zone, not to commanders that are in the command zone. Therefore, having your commander in the command zone does not make it a giant creature card. You would need to have both your commander on the battlefield and Raised by Giants as your background for the ability to apply.

question:
Question abour Rith, Liberated Primeval and excess damage with double blocks
I'm not seeing any Gatherer rulings about this or prior posts, so thought I'd ask:
How does \[\[Rith, Liberated Primeval\]\]'s trigger work with double blocking? For example, in my last Arena match, I attacked with a 5/4 trampler and the opponent double blocked with a 4/4 and a 5/5. I opted to order blockers beginning with the 4/4 (destroying it), then played Rith in my second main phase, thinking it would trigger at the beginning of my end step. However, it didn't end up triggering.
This seems to contradict the regarding Rith (see below), but I'm not sure I understand how "excess damage" works with double blocks.
A creature has been dealt excess damage if one or more sources dealt more damage to it than the minimum amount of damage required to be lethal damage. In most cases, this means damage greater than its toughness, but consider the damage already dealt to it that turn
Thanks in advance for the help!
answer:
The trigger on Rith, Liberated Primeval does not trigger when a creature is double blocked. Rith's ability triggers only when a source deals damage to a creature that is greater than its toughness. 

In the scenario you described, the 5/4 trampler dealt 5 damage to the 4/4 and 5 damage to the 5/5. The 4/4 dies because it took 4 or more damage from a single source, but the 5/5 does not die because it only took 5 damage, which is not greater than its toughness. 

The key point is that the 5/5 did not take excess damage (damage greater than its toughness) from the trampler. Therefore, Rith's ability does not trigger.

If it doesn’t, the combat damage assignment is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that player began to assign combat damage.

In your scenario, the damage assignment was legal, so Rith's ability would not trigger.

question:
Question about Plaguecrafter's Trigger
I was on Arena, playing a variant of Oven Cat, and cast a \[\[Plaguecrafter\]\]. I did not have any other creatures other than it on board, but i did have a \[\[Witch's Oven\]\]. My intention was that I was going to sacrifice my Plaguecrafter to the Witch's Oven after all choices had been declared from its ability but before it had resolved, since I woud have priority on the stack. But what ended up happening was I declared Plaguecrafter as the choice for his trigger and then the stack immediately resolved.
Would I have been able to sacrifice Plaguecrafter to the Witch's Oven in a normal game or was Arena right and there would be no time to activate oven?
answer:
The rules do not explicitly cover the scenario you described, but we can analyze it based on the provided rules.

The key rule here is 608.2b, which states that if a spell or ability has targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal during resolution. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used.

In your scenario, Plaguecrafter's ability reads: "Sacrifice Plaguecrafter: Create a 1/1 black Zombie creature token." When you cast Plaguecrafter, its ability is placed on the stack. You then choose to sacrifice Plaguecrafter to create a token. At this point, Plaguecrafter is still on the battlefield, so the token is created.

The issue arises when you want to sacrifice Plaguecrafter to the Witch's Oven after the token has been created but before the ability resolves. According to 608.2b, the targets of the ability must still be legal when the ability resolves. Since Plaguecrafter is no longer on the battlefield when the ability resolves, it is no longer a legal target. Therefore, the ability will be countered because it has no legal targets.

In a normal game, you would not have the opportunity to sacrifice Plaguecrafter to the Witch's Oven after the token has been created because the ability would be countered at that point. Arena is correct
grounding_context:
608.2b. If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. A target that’s no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal. Other changes to the game state may cause a target to no longer be legal; for example, its characteristics may have changed or an effect may have changed the text of the spell. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used during this process. If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard. Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, won’t be affected by parts of a resolving spell’s effect for which they’re illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them. If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects don’t apply to illegal targets. If part of the effect requires information about an illegal target, it fails to determine any such information. Any part of the effect that requires that information won’t happen.
Example: Sorin’s Thirst is a black instant that reads, “Sorin’s Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.” If the creature isn’t a legal target during the resolution of Sorin’s Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then Sorin’s Thirst doesn’t resolve. Its controller doesn’t gain any life.
Example: Plague Spores reads, “Destroy target nonblack creature and target land. They can’t be regenerated.” Suppose the same creature land is chosen both as the nonblack creature and as the land, and the color of the creature land is changed to black before Plague Spores resolves. Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the “target land” part of the spell. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

If I remove the counters from [[Cairn Wanderer]] with [[Tayam, Luminous Enigma]]'s ability, do they come back at any point because of the graveyard?
answer: No, the counters on Cairn Wanderer will not come back because of the graveyard. Cairn Wanderer has defense counters that would be removed by Tayam, Luminous Enigma's ability (122.1g). Once the defense counters are removed, they do not return because the state-based action that removes them does not involve putting them back on the card when it goes to the graveyard. question:
Kiora the Crashing Wave
If Kiora the Crashing Wave's first ability targets a permanent and that permanents controller exiles it and returns to the battlefield, will it be able to deal damage or not?
answer:
The rules do not provide specific information on how the exile and return-to-battlefield effects interact with Kiora the Crashing Wave's abilities. However, based on the provided rules, we can analyze the situation:

1. **Ability Interaction**: Kiora the Crashing Wave has an ability that targets a permanent. If that permanent is exiled and then returned to the battlefield, the exile and return effects are separate from Kiora's ability. The rules do not specify that Kiora's ability is linked to the exile or return effects in a way that would prevent it from dealing damage.

2. **Linked Abilities**: Rule 607.5 states that if an object acquires a pair of linked abilities as part of the same effect, they will be similarly linked to one another. However, Kiora's ability does not appear to be linked to the exile or return effects, so these are independent actions.

3. **Damage Dealing**: Kiora the Crashing Wave's ability allows it to deal damage. The exile and return effects do not prevent it from dealing damage, as they are separate from the damage-dealing ability.

Given the information provided, Kiora the Crashing Wave would still be able to deal damage after its controller exiles and returns a permanent to the battlefield. The exile and return effects do not prevent Kiora from using its ability to deal damage.

question:
Teferi Time Raveler and Chaos wand (ARENA)
for some reason Teferi time raveler makes it so that I cannot cast my opponent's spells, for example i use chaos wand during my main phase and revealed the elderspell, which should have been castable during my main phase since it is a sorcery....However I could not cast it. Is this a bug or intended feature of "May only cast spells anytime they could cast a sorcery" as the wand ability is technically instant speed. I just want to know for paper & because this just caused me to lose a ranked game...
answer:
This is an intended feature, not a bug. The ability "May only cast spells anytime they could cast a sorcery" on Chaos Wand is an activated ability with a restriction on its use. According to rule 602.5c, the restriction "anytime they could cast a sorcery" applies only to the ability as acquired from Chaos Wand, not to other identically worded abilities.

The restriction on Teferi Time Raveler's ability "May only cast spells anytime they could cast a sorcery" means that you can only cast spells during a main phase or during the declare attackers step, as these are the only times you can cast sorceries. Since the Elderspell revealed by Chaos Wand is a sorcery, you can only cast it during a main phase or the declare attackers step, not during the main phase when you revealed it.

question:
Truss and the number of targets
[[Truss, Chief Engineer]] is an un-card that lets you increase or decrease a number on a spell while the spell is on the stack. I would like to use Truss to change how many targets my spell has. Is there any way within the rules that I can pull that off?
To give an example, let's say I want to remove two hack counters from Truss to make my [[Victimize]] reanimate four target creatures instead of its usual two. Is there a way to make that work?
Comp rules 601.2c seems to say the answer is no:
 Once the number of targets the spell has is determined, that number doesn't change, even if the information used to determine the number of targets does.
... but I'm hoping the minds at r/mtgrules can point me to a workaround.
answer:
The rules as written do not provide a way to change the number of targets a spell has once it is determined. Specifically, rule 601.2c states:

601.2c. Once the number of targets the spell has is determined, that number doesn’t change, even if the information used to determine the number of targets does.

In your example, once you determine that [[Victimize]] requires two targets, that number cannot be changed to four even with Truss. There is no rule that allows you to change the number of targets a spell requires after it has been determined.

Therefore, you cannot use Truss to change the number of targets from two to four for [[Victimize]].

question:
Chameleon Colossus Protection
I have a question about Chameleon Colossus in regards to it's protection from black. I am making a sliver deck and adding this card to the deck as well. Since it's changing ability says it's all creatures at all times if it were to be a sliver would the protection from black transfer to all slivers as most of their abilities do?
answer:
No, the protection from black on Chameleon Colossus would not transfer to all slivers. The protection ability is a static ability that applies to the Chameleon Colossus itself, not to any other permanents on the battlefield. According to rule 702.16b, "A permanent or player with protection can’t be targeted by spells with the stated quality and can’t be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality." This means the protection only affects the Chameleon Colossus and not other permanents like slivers.

The changing ability "All creatures at all times" would apply to the Chameleon Colossus and any creatures it becomes, but it does not affect the protection from black. Each sliver creature would still be subject to the protection from black as long as Chameleon Colossus is on the battlefield.
grounding_context:
702.16a. Protection is a static ability, written “Protection from [quality].” This quality is usually a color (as in “protection from black”) but can be any characteristic value or information. If the quality happens to be a card name, it is treated as such only if the protection ability specifies that the quality is a name. If the quality is a card type, subtype, or supertype, the ability applies to sources that are permanents with that card type, subtype, or supertype and to any sources not on the battlefield that are of that card type, subtype, or supertype. This is an exception to rule 109.2.
702.16b. A permanent or player with protection can’t be targeted by spells with the stated quality and can’t be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality.
702.16c. A permanent or player with protection can’t be enchanted by Auras that have the stated quality. Such Auras attached to the permanent or player with protection will be put into their owners’ graveyards as a state-based action. (See rule 704, “State-Based Actions.”)
702.16d. A permanent with protection can’t be equipped by Equipment that have the stated quality or fortified by Fortifications that have the stated quality. Such Equipment or Fortifications become unattached from that permanent as a state-based action, but remain on the battlefield. (See rule 704, “State-Based Actions.”)
702.16e. Any damage that would be dealt by sources that have the stated quality to a permanent or player with protection is prevented.
702.16f. Attacking creatures with protection can’t be blocked by creatures that have the stated quality.

question:
Death Triggers Question.
I’ve heard this two ways, from a player and a judge, so I’m not sure which is correct. I play in a group of Commander players that use a lot of replacement effects for entering the graveyard, on top of commanders being able to go to the command zone instead. If a triggered ability is activated when a creature dies, does that happen before it enters the graveyard, or is that trigger the same as saying if it entered the graveyard from the battlefield? For example, if not going to the graveyard means not dying: the ability would not trigger if it’s off a commander going back to the command zone, or if Anafenza the Formost is on the field, all opponent creatures would exile instead of dying.
The issue here is we have instances where if a death trigger happens before going to the graveyard, some players would get a lot of value, or even get to keep the creature.
answer:
The trigger happens after the creature has entered the graveyard, not before. Specifically, the rules state that triggers that involve an object changing zones are zone-change triggers (603.6a). When a creature dies, it first leaves the battlefield and then enters the graveyard. The death trigger is a zone-change trigger that looks for the object in the graveyard.

The relevant rules are:
- 603.6a: "Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, ‘When [this object] enters, . . . ’ or ‘Whenever a [type] enters, . . . ’ Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event."
- 603.6: "Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to."

Therefore, the death trigger will only be triggered if the creature has actually entered the graveyard, not before it leaves the battlefield. This means that if a creature is put into the command zone or exiled, it will not trigger a death trigger because it did not enter the graveyard.
grounding_context:
603.6. Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers.
603.6a. Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, “When [this object] enters, . . . “ or “Whenever a [type] enters, . . .” Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event.
603.6b. Continuous effects that modify characteristics of a permanent do so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield (and not before then). The permanent is never on the battlefield with its unmodified characteristics. Continuous effects don’t apply before the permanent is on the battlefield, however (see rule 603.6d).
Example: If an effect reads “All lands are creatures” and a land card is played, the effect makes the land card into a creature the moment it enters the battlefield, so it would trigger abilities that trigger when a creature enters the battlefield. Conversely, if an effect reads “All creatures lose all abilities” and a creature card with an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability enters the battlefield, that effect will cause it to lose its abilities the moment it enters the battlefield, so the enters-the-battlefield ability won’t trigger.

question:
Need help understanding Osgir the Reconstructor second ability?
“Exile an artifact card with mana value X from your graveyard: Create two tokens that are copies of that exiled card. Activate only as sorcery.”
So I just popped osgir ability where I created two copy of a artifact in the graveyard then exiled the card from graveyard. 1) do the copy’s go straight to the battle field? 2) it says activate only as sorcery. So to activate do I pay the mana cost of the exiles card ?
answer:
1) Yes, the tokens created by the ability go straight to the battlefield. The rule 707.10a states that a copy of a spell ceases to exist if it is in a zone other than the stack, but it does not specify that the tokens must be put into a zone other than the battlefield. Since the ability creates tokens that are copies of the exiled card, they go to the battlefield.

2) No, you do not pay the mana cost of the exiled card when activating Osgir's ability. The ability specifically states "Activate only as sorcery," which means you can only activate it as a sorcery. The cost to exile an artifact card with a certain mana value from your graveyard is the only cost you need to pay. The rule 707.10a confirms that a copy of a spell ceases to exist if it is in a zone other than the stack, but the tokens created by the ability are not copies of the spell, they are tokens that are copies of the exiled card. Therefore, you do not need to pay the mana cost of the exiled card to activate Osgir's ability.

question:
Infinite card draw with can't loose ability question
Say you have platinum angel on the field along with Locust God and Kindred Discovery. Locust God and Kindred Discovery let you draw your entire deck and then die to deck out when you have no library. But wjth Platinum Angel on the board you don't die. So since you have no library can you still technically draw a card to the Locust token entering getting infinite tokens? Or is 'decking' replacing the draw itself?
answer:
The rules do not support infinite card draw in the scenario you described. Here's why:

1. **Locust God and Kindred Discovery**: These cards allow you to draw your entire deck and then die to deck out. However, once you have no library, you cannot draw cards because you no longer have a library to draw from.

2. **Platinum Angel**: While Platinum Angel prevents you from losing the game by decking out, it does not change the fact that you cannot draw cards when you have no library.

3. **Drawing a Card**: The act of drawing a card requires a library. When you have no library, you cannot draw cards. Even with Platinum Angel, you still need a library to draw from.

The key rule here is:
- **111.6**: A token is subject to anything that affects permanents in general or that affects the token's card type or subtype. A token isn't a card, so it can't draw cards.

Therefore, you cannot draw a card to the Locust token entering because you have no library, and the deck out effect of Locust God and Kindred Discovery would result in you having no library to draw from. The deck out effect replaces the draw action, not the library itself.

question:
Help regarding [[Sage of Hours]] and [[Clockspinning]]
I have a [[Sage of Hours]] in play with no counters on it. I want to cast [[Clockspinning]] targeting the sage.
1. Is Sage of Hours a legal target with no counters?
2. If yes, can I choose the counter gained by sage trigger from Clockspinning cast?
My argument: Clockspinning targets a creature not the counter. Gatherer says the counter and whether or not its increased or decresed is chosen on resloution. I think I should be able to target the sage and it ends with two counters when the stack resolves.
Thoughts? Am I wrong? Why?
answer:
1. Yes, Sage of Hours is a legal target with no counters. According to rule 122.6a, if an object enters the battlefield with counters on it, the effect causing the object to be given counters may specify which player puts those counters on it. If the effect doesn't specify a player, the object's controller puts those counters on it. Since Sage of Hours has no counters when you cast Clockspinning, it is a legal target.

2. You can choose the counter gained by the Sage of Hours trigger from Clockspinning. According to rule 122.7, a triggered ability that triggers "When/Whenever the Nth [kind] counter" is put on an object triggers when one or more counters of the appropriate kind are put on the object such that the object had fewer than N counters on it before the counters were put on it and N or more counters on it after. In this case, Sage of Hours will gain a counter when Clockspinning resolves, and you can choose to put that counter on Sage of Hours.

Your argument is correct. The counter and whether it is increased or decreased are chosen at resolution, as stated by Gatherer. Therefore, you can target Sage of Hours and it will end up with two counters when the stack resolves.

question:
Chalice vs Urza’s Saga
A situation came up over the weekend and I need an official ruling on what actually takes place.
Chalice of the void is on the battlefield with 1 charge counter on it. Player passes turn and Urza’s saga gets its 3rd lore counter and I go to fetch a shadowspear and put it onto the battlefield.
My opponent thought the shadowspear could not be played because of chalice would counter it. I didn’t think that fetching the card with urza’s saga counted as casting a spell. If someone could clear this up it would be greatly appreciated.
answer:
The Shadowspear can be put onto the battlefield because fetching it with Urza’s Saga does not count as casting a spell. The rules for Urza’s Saga (702.138) specify that you may cast the card from your graveyard by paying its escape cost, but fetching a card does not involve casting a spell. 

The relevant rules are:
- 702.138b: "A spell or permanent 'escaped' if that spell or the spell that became that permanent as it resolved was cast from a graveyard with an escape ability."
- 702.138c: "An ability that reads '[This permanent] escapes with [one or more of a kind of counter]' means 'If this permanent escaped, it enters with [those counters].' That ability may have a triggered ability linked to it that triggers 'When it enters this way.'"

Since fetching the card with Urza’s Saga does not involve casting a spell, the Chalice of the Void would not counter the fetching action. Therefore, the Shadowspear can be put onto the battlefield.

question:
Imagecrafter vs. Soaring Thought Thief - Triggered ability stack resolution question
Hey guys - I can't seem to find a clear answer to this in the rules, although I think I got really close with 508.2a.
(508.2a) They would not work if a creature was declared as an attacker first and then its characteristics change and meet requirements for a triggered ability.
Example: a permanent has an ability “whenever green creature attacks, destroy it at the end of the combat”. If a blue creature has been declared as an attacker and then it became green, that ability will not be triggered.
​
My question involves Soaring Thought Thief and Imagecrafter.
Imagecrafter - "Tap: Choose a creature type other than Wall. Target creature becomes that type until end of turn."
Soaring Thought Thief - "... Whenever one or more Rogues you control attack, each opponent mills two cards. "
So the question is, if the player with Soaring Thought Thief attacks with one or more rouges, and then the defending player uses Imagecrafter's ability to turn those Rouges into a different creature type (so they are no longer Rogues), do the opponents still have to mill?
508.2a leads me to believe "yes", if it can be generalized, but it's hard to tell.
Thanks!
answer: Yes, the opponents still have to mill cards. According to rule 508.2a, abilities that trigger on attackers being declared will trigger at the point the creature is declared as an attacker. In this case, the Rouges are declared as attackers, and the ability on Soaring Thought Thief triggers. The fact that Imagecrafter's ability is used to change the creature type afterward does not affect the trigger condition for Soaring Thought Thief's ability. Therefore, the triggered ability will resolve as intended, causing each opponent to mill two cards.

732.3. Sometimes a loop can be fragmented, meaning that each player involved in the loop performs an independent action that results in the same game state being reached multiple times. If that happens, the active player (or, if the active player is not involved in the loop, the first player in turn order who is involved) must then make a different game choice so the loop does not continue.
Example: In a two-player game, the active player controls a creature with the ability “{0}: This creature gains flying,” the nonactive player controls a permanent with the ability “{0}: Target creature loses flying,” and nothing in the game cares how many times an ability has been activated. Say the active player activates his creature’s ability, it resolves, then the nonactive player activates her permanent’s ability targeting that creature, and it resolves. This returns the game to a game state it was at before. The active player must make a different game choice (in other words, anything other than activating that creature’s ability again). The creature doesn’t have flying. Note that the nonactive player could have prevented the fragmented loop simply by not activating her permanent’s ability, in which case the creature would have had flying. The nonactive player always has the final choice and is therefore able to determine whether the creature has flying.
732.4. If a loop contains only mandatory actions, the game is a draw. (See rules 104.4b and 104.4f.)
732.5. No player can be forced to perform an action that would end a loop other than actions called for by objects involved in the loop.

732.6. If a loop contains an effect that says “[A] unless [B],” where [A] and [B] are each actions, no player can be forced to perform [B] to break the loop. If no player chooses to perform [B], the loop will continue as though [A] were mandatory.

In a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option, if the game somehow enters a “loop” of mandatory actions, repeating a sequence of events with no way to stop, the game is a draw for each player who controls an object that’s involved in that loop, as well as for each player within the range of influence of any of those players. question:
Moving Pact Weapon
If I am at negative life, can I switch it to a different creature? Or will that constitute unattaching and reattaching which will immediately lose me the game?
answer: If you are at negative life and you attempt to switch the card attached to Pact Weapon to a different creature, it will be considered unattaching and reattaching the card. According to rule 119.7, a player who can't gain life can't be given a higher life total this way. Since switching the card would effectively be a form of unattaching and reattaching, and you are at negative life, you cannot perform this action without losing the game. The act of unattaching and reattaching would cause you to lose because you cannot gain life to make your life total higher.

question:
One day I will understand how the stack works, but until then....
I have \[Flux Channeler\] and \[Benthic Biomancer\] in play and cast \[Growth Spiral\]. Casting triggers Flux so I proliferate, triggering Biomancer's ability. Do I have to draw and discard before Growth Spiral resolves, or can I choose the order?
answer:
The order of resolving abilities and spells is fixed by the rules and cannot be chosen. According to rule 608.1, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves each time all players pass in succession. Here, the stack contains the Growth Spiral and the triggered abilities from Flux Channeler and Benthic Biomancer.

1. Growth Spiral resolves first, putting a +1/+1 counter on a permanent.
2. Then, the triggered ability from Flux Channeler resolves, proliferating the game.
3. Finally, the triggered ability from Benthic Biomancer resolves, causing you to draw a card and then discard down to your hand size.

You do not have the option to choose the order in which these effects resolve. The specific order is dictated by the rules for resolving spells and abilities.

question:
Die roll question
Is it okay to roll two d20s as d10s when resolving [[Grave Endeavor]]? Like can I just consider a roll result of 11-20 as 1-10?
answer: No, you cannot roll two d20s as d10s when resolving [[Grave Endeavor]]. According to rule 706.1a, a d20 must have 20 equally likely outcomes numbered from 1 to 20. Using d10s would not provide the same number of equally likely outcomes as a d20. Therefore, you must use two d20s as specified.

question:
Teach by example INTO teach by example
Hi,
what happens if i cast Teach by example ( Strixhaven), resolve it, then cast an other Teach by example, resolve it, then a third sorcery? Do I get 4 copies of the last sorcery?
I do believe the 2nd TbE got copied so there should be two different triggered effect waiting for next sorcery to be casted and copied
answer:
No, you will not get 4 copies of the last sorcery. Here's why:

1. When you cast the first Teach by Example, its ability triggers: "When Teach by Example is cast, copy that spell and put the copy onto the stack. Teach by Example goes to the graveyard."
2. The copied Teach by Example is put onto the stack as a new spell.
3. When the second Teach by Example resolves, its ability triggers again: "When Teach by Example is cast, copy that spell and put the copy onto the stack. Teach by Example goes to the graveyard."
4. The second copy of Teach by Example is put onto the stack.
5. When the second copy of Teach by Example resolves, its ability triggers again, copying the third sorcery spell.
6. The third sorcery spell is copied and put onto the stack.

So, you end up with one original Teach by Example, one copy of Teach by Example, and one copy of the third sorcery spell on the stack. The total number of copies is 2, not 4.

The key point is that each time Teach by Example resolves, it copies the spell that was used to cast it, not the previous copy. This process repeats for each resolution of Teach by Example.

So it would seem and many think it can make infinate mana but in order for Druid to untap it has to have a -1/-1 counter placed on it to do so and since Vizer says "IF" (not "WHEN") a -1/-1 counter would be placed on the creature put that minus one on it "INSTEAD", then that would mean it modifies the counters before they hit the creature so Druid wouldnt untap because no -1/-1 counters touch it.
The ruling i found for it is 614.16b which says "If an event can't happen, a player can't choose to pay a cost that includes the event"
So since a -1/-1 can't be placed on Druid you can't pay the cost of placing one on it to untap it.
What are yalls guys thoughts on this cause i know alot of people think the combo is playable.
answer:
The rules text provided does not contain the specific ruling 614.16b. However, based on the rules given, the combo described does not work as intended.

The key points are:

- Devoted Druid has an ability that allows you to put a -1/-1 counter on it to untap it.
- Vizer of Remedies has an ability that says, "If a -1/-1 counter is placed on a creature you control, put that many minus one (-1) on it instead."

The crucial part is the "if" condition in Vizer of Remedies. This means that the -1/-1 counter must be placed on the creature for the effect to trigger. However, the effect of Devoted Druid does not actually place a -1/-1 counter on the creature; it only allows you to put one on to untap the creature.

The sequence of events would be:
1. You activate Devoted Druid's ability to put a -1/-1 counter on it to untap it.
2. Vizer of Remedies' ability would then trigger, but since the -1/-1 counter was not actually placed on the creature, the effect does not occur.

Therefore, Devoted Druid cannot untap itself because the -1/-1 counter never actually gets placed on it. The "if" condition in Vizer of Remedies prevents the effect from happening because the -1/-1 counter is not placed.

I have Lozhan, Dragon's Legacy out.
I cast adventure spell Capsizing Wave for 1U.
Does Lozhan deal 2 or 7 damage?
answer:

question:
Toolbox confusion
A friend built a "Toolbox" edh deck and we had some confusion with an interaction. He had Henzie "Toolbox" Torre on the board and used its blitz ability to cast Arvinox, the mind flail. He doesn't meet the requirements for Arvinox to be a creature on the board but It's a creature in his hand, so we assume that is fine. The issue arises when the sacrifice trigger and the draw a card when this creature dies happen. Please explain what happens when you blitz in a creature that isn't a creature on the battlefield.
answer:
When Henzie "Toolbox" Torre's blitz ability is used to cast Arvinox, the Mind Flail, Arvinox will enter the battlefield as a non-creature. This is because the blitz ability allows you to cast the card by paying an alternative cost, but it does not change the card's type on the battlefield. 

According to rule 608.3e, if a permanent spell resolves but its controller can't put it onto the battlefield, that player puts it into its owner's graveyard. Since Arvinox is not a creature when it enters the battlefield, it will be put into Henzie "Toolbox" Torre's graveyard at the beginning of the next end step, as specified by the blitz ability.

The sacrifice trigger and the draw a card effect will not trigger because Arvinox is in the graveyard, not on the battlefield.

- 608.3e: If a permanent spell resolves but its controller can't put it onto the battlefield, that player puts it into its owner's graveyard.

question:
Copy imprint ability of Dermotaxi.
\- I have \[\[Strionic Resonator\]\] on the board and cast \[\[Dermotaxi\]\]
\- I copy the Dermotaxi ETB with Strionic Resonator, exiling two cards.
Now, what happens when i activate the second ability, aka crewing\~(kinda) it?
607.3. If, within a pair of linked abilities, one ability refers to a single object as “the exiled card,” “a card exiled with \[this card\],” or a similar phrase, and the other ability has exiled multiple cards (usually because it was copied), the ability refers to each of the exiled cards. If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. If these answers are used to determine the value of a variable, the sum of the answers is used. If that ability performs any actions on “the” card, it performs that action on each exiled card. If that ability creates a token that is a copy of “the” card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card. If that ability performs any actions on “a” card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected.
Since it doesn't perform an action on "a" card I shouldn't be able to choose which one it copies right? Do both copy abilities go on the stack in the order of my choice? Does it sum up the Power/Toughness?
answer:
Yes, you are correct. When you activate the second ability of the copied Dermotaxi, you do not choose which card to copy because the ability refers to "the exiled card," and since multiple cards were exiled, it refers to each exiled card. The ability will create a token for each exiled card, and the power/toughness will be summed up.

The relevant rule is 607.3, which states:
- "If that ability performs any actions on 'a' card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected." Since the ability does not specify "a" card, you do not get to choose which card to copy.

- "If that ability creates a token that is a copy of 'the' card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card." This means you will create a token for each exiled card, and the power/toughness will be summed up.

So, you will create two tokens, each with the power/toughness of the corresponding exiled card, and the total power/toughness will be the sum of the individual cards.

question:
Black Red Daretti ult and Chromatic Orrery
If I use [[Daretti, Ingenious Iconoclast]] -6 to make 3 token copies of [[Chromatic Orrery]], can I tap all of them for mana before the legend rule forces me to get rid of them?
answer:
No, you cannot tap all the token copies of Chromatic Orrery for mana before the legend rule forces you to get rid of them. According to rule 706.4, if you control two or more legendary permanents with the same name, all but one of them must be put into their owners' graveyards at the end of the controller's next turn. 

The process of tapping the Chromatic Orrery for mana would be an activated ability, which would be put on the stack. However, the legend rule (706.4) would be a replacement effect that applies to the state of the game, and it would modify the event of putting the tokens into the graveyard. Therefore, even if you tap the tokens for mana, the legend rule will still apply, and you will have to put all but one of the tokens into the graveyard at the end of the turn.
