question:
Choosing which simultaneous damage is prevented
I've come across an odd scenario:
Player 1 is attacking with \[\[Etrata, the Silencer\]\] and another evasive creature with 4 power (total of 7)
Player 2 has \[\[Palliation Accord\]\] in play with 6 shield counters (after gaining 2 from the attack) and a creature.
Palliation Accord reads "Remove a shield counter from \[this\]: Prevent the next 1 damage that would be dealt to you this turn"
Of the 7 simultaneous damage, 1 point will get through. Which player gets to decide whether Etrata deals 1 damage and triggers her ability, or the other creature deals 1 damage and she doesn't trigger?
answer: The player who controls the creature with Palliation Accord gets to decide which damage is prevented. According to rule 615.7, when damage would be dealt to the "shielded" permanent or player by two or more applicable sources at the same time, the player or the controller of the permanent chooses which damage the shield prevents. In this case, the damage from Etrata and the other creature are simultaneous and applicable sources of damage to Player 2. Therefore, Player 2 can choose which 1 damage to prevent.
grounding_context:
615.7. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to a specific amount of damage—for example, “Prevent the next 3 damage that would be dealt to any target this turn.” These work like shields. Each 1 damage that would be dealt to the “shielded” permanent or player is prevented. Preventing 1 damage reduces the remaining shield by 1. If damage would be dealt to the shielded permanent or player by two or more applicable sources at the same time, the player or the controller of the permanent chooses which damage the shield prevents. Once the shield has been reduced to 0, any remaining damage is dealt normally. Such effects count only the amount of damage; the number of events or sources dealing it doesn’t matter.
615.8. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to the next time a specific source would deal damage. These effects prevent the next instance of damage from that source, regardless of how much damage that is. Once an instance of damage from that source has been prevented, any subsequent instances of damage that would be dealt by that source are dealt normally.
615.9. Some effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability prevent damage from a source of a player’s choice with certain properties. When the source would deal damage, the shield rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced and the shield isn’t used up. See rule 609.7b.
615.10. Some prevention effects generated by static abilities refer to a specific amount of damage—for example, “If a source would deal damage to you, prevent 1 of that damage.” Such an effect prevents only the indicated amount of damage in any applicable damage event at any given time. It will apply separately to damage from other applicable events that would happen at the same time, or at a different time.
Example: Daunting Defender says “If a source would deal damage to a Cleric creature you control, prevent 1 of that damage.” Pyroclasm says “Pyroclasm deals 2 damage to each creature.” Pyroclasm will deal 1 damage to each Cleric creature controlled by Daunting Defender’s controller. It will deal 2 damage to each other creature.

Related rules:
609.7b. Some effects from resolved spells and abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties, such as a creature or a source of a particular color. When the source would deal damage, the “shield” rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced. If for any reason the shield prevents no damage or replaces no damage, the shield isn’t used up.

question:
Golos mutate deck
Hey everyone I'm creating a golos deck and am interested in mutate cards, am I able to mutate from golos' exile and play from exile effect?
answer: No, you cannot mutate from Golos' exile and play from exile effect. According to the rules, mutate cards must be cast from the hand or the stack, not from exile. Specifically, rule 702.140a states that "Mutate [cost]” means "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell’s mana cost. If you do, it becomes a mutating creature spell and targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as this spell." This clearly indicates that the spell must be in your hand or on the stack to use its mutate ability. Exile is not a valid zone for casting a spell with mutate.
grounding_context:

It’s written as “Companion—[Condition].” Before the game begins, you may reveal one card you own from outside the game with a companion ability whose condition is fulfilled by your starting deck. (See rule 103.2b.) Once during the game, any time you have priority and the stack is empty, but only during a main phase of your turn, you may pay {3} and put that card into your hand. This is a special action that doesn’t use the stack (see rule 116.2g). This is a change from previous rules.
702.139b. If a companion ability refers to your starting deck, it refers to your deck after you’ve set aside any sideboard cards. In a Commander game, this is also before you’ve set aside your commander.
702.139c. Once you take the special action and put the card with companion into your hand, it remains in the game until the game ends.
702.139d. Cards can enter Commander games from outside the game via the companion special action.
702.140. Mutate
702.140a. Mutate appears on some creature cards. It represents a static ability that functions while the spell with mutate is on the stack. “Mutate [cost]” means “You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell’s mana cost. If you do, it becomes a mutating creature spell and targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as this spell.” Casting a spell using its mutate ability follows the rules for paying alternative costs (see 601.2b and 601.2f–h).
702.140b. As a mutating creature spell begins resolving, if its target is illegal, it ceases to be a mutating creature spell and continues resolving as a creature spell and will be put onto the battlefield under the control of the spell’s controller.

Rather, it merges with the target creature and becomes one object represented by more than one card or token (see rule 730, “Merging with Permanents”). question:
Galea & equipment recursion
If I've cast an equipment with [[Galea, Kindler of Hope]], then the equipment gets destroyed and I re-cast the equipment from my graveyard...does the equipment retain the "when this equipment ETBs, attach to a creature you control" ?
answer: Yes, the equipment retains the "when this equipment ETBs, attach to a creature you control" ability. According to rule 301.5e, if an effect attempts to put an Equipment onto the battlefield attached to an object it can't legally equip, the Equipment enters the battlefield unattached. However, this rule does not apply to the specific "when this equipment ETBs, attach to a creature you control" ability. This ability is part of the Equipment's text and will remain with the Equipment even if it returns from the graveyard. The ability is not dependent on the Equipment being attached to a creature when it enters the battlefield, but rather is triggered when the Equipment enters the battlefield as an Equipment. Therefore, the Equipment will retain this ability when it returns from the graveyard.

Changing control of the creature doesn’t change control of the Equipment, and vice versa. Only the Equipment’s controller can activate its abilities. However, if the Equipment grants an ability to the equipped creature (with “gains” or “has”), the equipped creature’s controller is the only one who can activate that ability.
301.5e. If an effect attempts to put an Equipment that isn’t also an Aura (see rule 303.4i) onto the battlefield attached to either an object it can’t legally equip or an object that is undefined, the Equipment enters the battlefield unattached. If the Equipment is a token, it’s created and enters the battlefield unattached.
301.5f. An ability of a permanent that refers to the “equipped creature” refers to whatever creature that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isn’t an Equipment.

How does Runic Armasaur interact with Urza, Lord High Artificer?
Specifically, does \[\[Runic Armasaur\]\] trigger when an opponent uses \[\[Urza, Lord High Artificer\]\] to tap an artifact for mana?
answer:
No, Runic Armasaur does not trigger when an opponent uses Urza, Lord High Artificer to tap an artifact for mana. 

The key rule here is 605.4a, which states that a triggered mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Runic Armasaur’s afterlife ability would trigger if a permanent it controls is put into the graveyard from the battlefield, but tapping an artifact for mana does not put a permanent into the graveyard. Therefore, Runic Armasaur’s afterlife ability would not be triggered in this scenario.

question:
Paying into X spells more mana than there are valid Targets
Hoping someone can clarify this for me as nothing useful was coming up in google searches. I have a Commander deck helmed by \[\[Zaxara, the Exemplary\]\] so there are a good number of X spells in the deck. My question is, can I pay into an X spell more mana than there are targets?
Example: I want to cast \[\[Curse of the Swine\]\] which has the wording "Exile X target creatures". I have 10 mana I can spend, but there are only 4 creatures on the battlefield. Spending the 10 mana would get me a 8/8 Hydra via Zaxara since X = 8. Is this valid, or can I only pay into X the number of valid targets there are? I know for other cards like \[\[Hex\]\] you have to have 6 different valid targets in order to even be able to cast it.
​
I actually just thought of another question when writing this. If I cast Hex while there are 6 valid targets, then someone sacrifices one of the targets and now there are only 5 legal targets, does Hex still resolve?
​
Thanks!
answer:
The rules do not explicitly state that you can only pay into X the number of valid targets. Instead, the rules focus on the targeting and cost requirements of spells.

For your first question: Yes, you can pay into X more mana than there are valid targets. The rules do not restrict the amount of mana you can pay into an X spell based on the number of valid targets. You can pay the full cost of the spell, and if there are not enough targets, the spell will still resolve to the extent that it can. In your example, you can pay 10 mana to "Curse of the Swine," and it will exile 8 creatures, creating an 8/8 Hydra via Zaxara, even though there are only 4 creatures on the battlefield.

For your second question: If you cast "Hex" with 6 valid targets, and one of those targets is sacrificed, reducing the number of valid targets to 5, the spell will still resolve. "Hex" will exile 5 creatures, and the spell will still resolve to the extent that it can. The spell will not be countered or removed from the stack because of the reduction in the number of targets; it will simply resolve with fewer targets than it initially targeted.

In summary, the rules do not limit the amount of mana you can pay into an X spell based on the number of valid targets. The spell will resolve to the extent that it can, regardless of the number of targets.

question:
Legend rule question.
If I make a token of something like [[Lena, Selfless Champion]] with a sacrifice ability, am I able to use that ability before I sacrifice it to the legend rule? Like does the legend rule go on the stack like I'm thinking?
answer:
The Legend rule does not go on the stack. Instead, it is a replacement effect that modifies the event of putting a legendary permanent onto the battlefield. The relevant rules are:

- **616.1a**: If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects are self-replacement effects, one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1b.
- **616.1g**: While following the steps in 616.1a–f, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen.

In the case of Lena, Selfless Champion, when you create a token, the ability "As this creature enters the battlefield, sacrifice it" is a replacement effect that applies to the event of putting the token onto the battlefield. This effect must be chosen before the token is actually put onto the battlefield, and it cannot be countered or responded to because it is a replacement effect, not a spell or ability on the stack.

Therefore, you cannot use the sacrifice ability before the token is put onto the battlefield to avoid the Legend rule. The Legend rule will trigger if you put a second legendary creature of the same name onto the battlefield.

question:
Immursturm Predator
If I attack with [[Immursturm Predator]], am I able to use its sacrifice-gain indestructible ability? Or does already being tapped prevent this as “tap it” is a condition of the ability? Thanks 😁
answer: The ability on Immursturm Predator states: "Sacrifice Immursturm Predator: It gains indestructible until end of turn." This ability does not have a tap condition, so you can activate it even though the creature is already tapped from attacking. The ability to sacrifice the creature to gain indestructible is separate from the act of attacking, which only requires tapping the creature. Therefore, you can use the ability to give Immursturm Predator indestructible. Rule 508.1h confirms that once the total cost is determined, it becomes "locked in," and you can activate the ability after paying the cost to attack. Rule numbers 508.1h and 508.1i support this interpretation.

question:
Distant Melody + Creatures entering the battlefield during casting
Hello everyone I need help with the following, if I have \[\[Kykar, Wind's Fury\]\] on the battlefield (no other creatures) and cast \[\[Distant Melody\]\] choosing spirits
Will I draw at least one card because Kykar ability triggers before Distant Melody resolves and one spirit will be on the battelfield
Or does Distant Melody "checks" the creatures types I control when is cast, thus drawing nothing because there is no spirit at that moment on the battelfield
Thank you in advance!
answer:
Distant Melody will not draw a card in this scenario. Here's why:

1. **Distant Melody's Trigger**: Distant Melody has an ability that triggers when a spirit enters the battlefield under your control. This trigger is an event that occurs when the card is cast and placed on the stack, not when it resolves.

2. **Timing of Events**: When you cast Distant Melody, it checks the types of creatures you control at the time of casting. At that moment, you have no creatures on the battlefield, including no spirits. Therefore, the trigger condition is not met.

3. **Triggered Ability**: The trigger "When a spirit enters the battlefield under your control" is an event that happens after the card is cast and before it resolves. It does not affect the card's casting or resolution process.

4. **Rule Reference**: This behavior is consistent with how triggered abilities work. They are events that happen after the spell or ability is cast but before it resolves. The relevant rule here is:
   - **509.1a**: An ability that triggers only when a specified event occurs on a permanent, as opposed to an ability that triggers when a permanent with that ability changes from one state to another, is an event trigger. Event triggers trigger only when their trigger event occurs.

Therefore, Distant Melody will not draw a card because the trigger condition is not met when the card is cast. The trigger will only be able to function

question:
Devoid
Hi,
Couple of friends got into a giant argument over this: can I run colored cards with Devoid in a Kozilek edh deck?
answer:
No, you cannot run colored cards with Devoid in a Kozilek EDH deck. Devoid states that an object "becomes colorless" if it would become any color. Since Kozilek, The Seer of Logic is a colorless planeswalker, its color identity is undefined. Therefore, any card with Devoid would become colorless, preventing it from being any color, including the colors required by Kozilek's color identity.

The relevant rules are:
- 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity. This is an exception to rule 712.8a."
- 903.4e: "If an ability refers to the colors or number of colors in a commander’s color identity, that quality is undefined if that player doesn’t have a commander. That part of the ability won’t do anything. Costs that refer to that quality are unpayable."

Since Devoid would make the card colorless, it cannot be any color, thus preventing it from matching Kozilek's color identity.

question:
Blocking damage???
I can’t believe I need to ask this - but I’ve been playing MTG Arena and with everything done automatically when I was trying to show my girlfriend how magic works today I couldn’t remember - then I tried looking it up and it was taking too long and frustrating me. So when a 2/1 creature attacks and is blocked by a 2/1creature, the attacking creature kills the blocking creature right? They don’t destroy each other correct? If a 2/1 is blocked by a 2/2 creature then they are both destroyed, yes? What is the rule or a way I can remember the blocking dynamics?
Thanks, sorry sorry such a basic question.
answer:
In Magic: The Gathering, when a creature is blocked, the blocking creature assigns its combat damage to the attacking creature, and then the attacking creature assigns its combat damage to the blocking creature. The combat damage is assigned simultaneously, and the life totals are reduced accordingly.

For your specific examples:

1. If a 2/1 creature attacks and is blocked by a 2/1 creature, each creature will assign 2 damage to the other. Both creatures will die because 2 damage is equal to their power, and they will each lose 2 life. The game state will be that both creatures are destroyed.

2. If a 2/1 creature attacks and is blocked by a 2/2 creature, the 2/2 will assign 2 damage to the 2/1. The 2/1 will assign 1 damage to the 2/2. The 2/1 will die because it loses 2 life, but the 2/2 will only lose 1 life and survive.

The key rule here is 510.1c, which states that a blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it, and an unblocked creature assigns its combat damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it’s attacking.

Remember, the damage is assigned simultaneously, and the life totals are reduced at the same time. The creatures are not destroyed by each other; they are simply dealt damage. The life totals are what determine if

510.1. First, the active player announces how each attacking creature assigns its combat damage, then the defending player announces how each blocking creature assigns its combat damage. 510.1a. Each attacking creature and each blocking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power. Creatures that would assign 0 or less damage this way don’t assign combat damage at all.
510.1b. An unblocked creature assigns its combat damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it’s attacking. If it isn’t currently attacking anything (if, for example, it was attacking a planeswalker that has left the battlefield), it assigns no combat damage.
510.1c. A blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it. If no creatures are currently blocking it (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If two or more creatures are blocking it, it assigns its combat damage to those creatures divided as its controller chooses among them.
Example: An attacking Elvish Regrower (a 4/3 creature) is blocked by Vampire Spawn (a 2/3 creature) and Helpful Hunter (a 1/1 creature). Elvish Regrower’s controller can assign all 4 damage to the Hunter, 1 damage to the Spawn and 3 damage to the Hunter, 2 damage to each creature, 3 damage to the Spawn and 1 damage to the Hunter, or all 4 damage to the Spawn.

question:
Gaining Control of Someone's Commander Then Flicking to Keep
I'm pretty sure I'm right, but I want to make sure before I start doing it in games. If I take control of somebody's commander with, say, \[\[Willbreaker\]\] then use something to flick it to my side like \[\[Conjurer's Closet\]\] or \[\[Thassa, Deep-Dwelling\]\] it would still be considered that player's commander and therefore will still deal commander damage, right? I know if you transform the commander in some way, say Oko's elking, it still deals commander damage, but I've never seen someone take control then flick before.
My thought process:
903.3. Each deck has a legendary creature card designated as its commander. This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself. The card retains this designation even when it changes zones.
Because it's an attribute it just innately is the commander.
However, other cards become new instances if otherwise returned to the field. A permanent returning is considered an entirely new object with no memory of its previous existence.
This feels wrong though because, at least how I understand it, it's still innately the commander. It's not that it's a new version of that creature. It's not forgetting it's a commander, it just is.
Fun side thought scenario:
Two Kenrith decks fighting, one has Willbreaker and takes control of their opponent's Kenrith. The thief sacs their own Kenrith so they can keep their opponent's, bounces it, and now hits the original Kenrith's owner until lethal. Remember, kids. Always have a \[\[Homeward Path\]\] or speak to your nearest store manager to find your parents.
answer:
Yes, your understanding is correct. When you take control of an opponent's commander with a card like Willbreaker, and then use a card like Conjurer's Closet or Thassa, Deep-Dwelling to "flick" it to your side, the card still retains its status as the original player's commander. 

The key rule here is 903.3, which states that the designation of a card as a commander is an attribute of the card itself, not a characteristic of the object it represents. Therefore, even though the card changes zones, it still retains its status as the original player's commander.

The example you provided with Willbreaker and the subsequent use of Conjurer's Closet or Thassa, Deep-Dwelling to "flick" the card to your side is a valid scenario. The card will still deal commander damage to the original owner, as it is still considered their commander.

For the fun side thought scenario:
- If you take control of your opponent's Kenrith with Willbreaker, and then use Conjurer's Closet to "flick" it to your side, the Kenrith still deals commander damage to the original owner.
- You can sacrifice your own Kenrith to use Willbreaker, take control of the opponent's Kenrith, "flick" it to your side, and then use it to deal commander damage to the original owner.

The rules support this interpretation, so you are correct in your understanding.

question:
Drown in the Loch to counter a Delved Murktide Regent
Player A casts \[\[Murktide Regent\]\], exiling X cards from their graveyard using Delve.
Player B casts \[\[Drown in the Loch\]\] to attempt to counter Murktide Regent.
Are the X cards exiled with Delve counted by Drown in the Loch's number-of-cards-in-graveyard condition, or are they not counted because they have been exiled to pay Murktide Regen't mana cost?
Thanks
answer: The X cards exiled with Delve are not counted by Drown in the Loch's number-of-cards-in-graveyard condition. According to rule 702.66, the delve ability allows you to exile a card from your graveyard rather than pay the corresponding mana, but these exiled cards are not in your graveyard for the purposes of Drown in the Loch's condition. Drown in the Loch specifically checks the number of cards in your graveyard, and since the cards were exiled to pay the cost, they do not meet this condition.

question:
Can I sacrifice Carrion Feeder to itself
If I have a [[carrion feeder]] and [[Marchesa, the Black Rose]] on the battlefield can I sacrifice the feeder to itself to put a +1/+1 counter on itself and then get the feeder to come back at the next end step or do I need to have a separate creature each time to sac to the feeder
answer:
No, you cannot sacrifice Carrion Feeder to itself to put a +1/+1 counter on itself and then have it come back at the next end step. The rules for Carrion Feeder's ability (603.12a) state that if the trigger event (sacrificing another creature) occurs multiple times during the resolution of the spell or ability that created it, the reflexive triggered ability will trigger only once for each of those times. 

In this case, sacrificing Carrion Feeder to itself would not count as sacrificing another creature, so the reflexive triggered ability would not trigger at all. You would need to sacrifice Carrion Feeder to a different creature to trigger the ability and put a +1/+1 counter on it, and then it would come back at the next end step according to Marchesa, the Black Rose's ability. 

Rules cited: 603.12a

answer:
The answer is that your opponent loses 11 life and you gain 11 life. According to rule 810.9, damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually, but the result is applied to the team's shared life total. 

In this scenario, the falkenrath's ability would deal 11 damage to each player. Since you are on the same team, the damage is applied to your team's shared life total. Therefore, your team loses 11 life, and you gain 11 life.

Specifically, rule 810.9 states: "Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total." This means that even though the falkenrath's ability targets each player individually, the damage is applied to the team's shared life total.

question:
Naban Trigger Question
Naban reads: "If a Wizard entering the battlefield under your control causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time."
So it's obvious this works with Wizard ETB triggers. But would it also work with cards that read, "Whenever you cast a blue spell..." If that blue spell is a Wizard. Cards such as Diamond Mare, Gadwick, the Wizened and so on.
Cheers!
answer:
The rule in Naban would apply to cards with triggers that occur when a Wizard enters the battlefield under your control, such as those with Wizard ETB triggers. However, it would not apply to cards with triggers that occur when you cast a blue spell, even if that spell is a Wizard. The key is in the timing and the specific trigger event.

The relevant rule is 603.2e, which states:
- "Some trigger events use the word ‘becomes’ (for example, ‘becomes attached’ or ‘becomes blocked’). These trigger only at the time the named event happens—they don’t trigger if that state already exists or retrigger if it persists. An ability that triggers when a permanent ‘becomes tapped’ or ‘becomes untapped’ doesn’t trigger if the permanent enters the battlefield in that state."

In the case of Naban, the trigger is specifically tied to a Wizard entering the battlefield, which is a clear and distinct event. The triggers for cards like Diamond Mare, Gadwick, the Wizened, etc., are tied to casting a blue spell, which is a different event.

Therefore, Naban would not trigger for cards with "Whenever you cast a blue spell" triggers because those triggers are not tied to a Wizard entering the battlefield.

An ability that triggers when a permanent “becomes tapped” or “becomes untapped” doesn’t trigger if the permanent enters the battlefield in that state.
Example: An ability that triggers when a permanent “becomes tapped” triggers only when the status of a permanent that’s already on the battlefield changes from untapped to tapped.

question:
Does a Copy have its cmc or it'd copied cmc when it dies?
I have a [[Cursed Mirror]] that copied an [[Angel of the Ruins]], attacked, and died. I control [[Scrap Trawler]]. Do I get to return an artifact card of mana value 2 or less (because Mirror is cost 3) or do I get to return mana value 6 or less (since Mirror was copying a 7 CMC card as it died)?
Thanks in advance!
answer:
The Copy's mana value at the time of death determines the cost of the card you can return with Scrap Trawler. According to rule 202.3, the mana value of the copy is determined by the copiable values of the face that's currently up. When the Copy of Angel of the Ruins died, it would have been copying the Angel of the Ruins, which has a mana cost of {4} (CMC of 4). Therefore, the Copy's mana value at the time of death would be 4.

The relevant rules are:
- 707.8: "When copying a melded permanent or other double-faced permanent, use the copiable values of the face that’s currently up to determine the characteristics of the copy."
- 202.3: "The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0, unless that object is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell, or it is a melded permanent."

Since the Copy was copying Angel of the Ruins, its mana value at the time of death would be 4, not the 7 CMC of the Angel of the Ruins. Therefore, you can return an artifact card with a mana value of 4 or less, not 6 or less.

So, you can return an artifact card with a mana value of 2 or less, as specified by Scrap Trawler.
grounding_context:
202.3. The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color.
Example: A mana cost of {3}{U}{U} translates to a mana value of 5.
202.3a. The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0, unless that object is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell, or it is a melded permanent.
202.3b. The mana value of the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell’s back face is calculated as though it had the mana cost of its front face. If a permanent or spell is a copy of the back face of a nonmodal double-faced object (even if the card representing that copy is itself a double-faced card), the mana value of the copy is 0.
Example: Huntmaster of the Fells is a nonmodal double-faced card with mana cost {2}{R}{G}. Its mana value is 4. After it transforms to its other face (Ravager of the Fells), its mana value remains 4.
Example: A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Ravager of the Fells. Its mana value is 0.
Example: Insectile Aberration is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced card whose front face has mana cost {U}. It becomes a copy of Ravager of the Fells. Its mana value becomes 0.
202.3c. The mana value of a melded permanent is calculated as though it had the combined mana cost of the front faces of each card that represents it. If a permanent is a copy of a melded permanent (even if that copy is represented by two other meld cards), the mana value of the copy is 0.

202.3e. When calculating the mana value of an object with an {X} in its mana cost, X is treated as 0 while the object is not on the stack, and X is treated as the number chosen for it while the object is on the stack.

Example: The mana value of a card with mana cost {1}{W/U}{W/U} is 3.
Example: The mana value of a card with mana cost {2/B}{2/B}{2/B} is 6.

question:
Flicker a Creature to save from a Target Removal Spell
Im kinda new to magic and im not familiar with this rule but can you really cast a Ghostly Flicker ( or any flicker effect) on a creature to fizzle the target removal spell?
answer:
The rules do not explicitly cover the scenario of using a Flicker effect to "fizzle" a target removal spell. However, the general principle of using a Flicker effect to save a creature from a target removal spell can be inferred from the rules.

The key rule here is:
- **701.11a. Flicker**: "Flicker" is a keyword action. "Flicker [card name]” means "Exile the card with that name and, at the beginning of the next end step, put that card into its owner’s hand." 

To apply this to your scenario:
1. You can use a Flicker effect to exile the targeted creature.
2. At the beginning of the next end step, the creature will be returned to your hand.

However, the target removal spell will still have resolved, meaning the effect of the removal spell will have been applied. The Flicker effect does not negate the removal effect; it merely prevents the creature from being put into the graveyard.

So, while you can use a Flicker effect to save a creature from being put into the graveyard, the removal effect will still have occurred. The specific rules cited do not cover the interaction between Flicker and target removal spells, but the general mechanics of Flicker can be used to save a creature from being removed.

702.34a. Flashback appears on some instants and sorceries. It represents two static abilities: one that functions while the card is in a player’s graveyard and another that functions while the card is on the stack. “Flashback [cost]” means “You may cast this card from your graveyard if the resulting spell is an instant or sorcery spell by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost” and “If the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack.” Casting a spell using its flashback ability follows the rules for paying alternative costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h.

question:
Noob Question - Instant Priority
I am playing against my wife,
It is my turn and she has a "shifting ceratops with 5/4"
I used a 4 damage instant on my main phase 1, she countered with her own instant Giant growth after seeing me cast the instant on her dinosaur.
My question is, which instant takes priority?
Do I reduce her toughness to 0 and she loses the ceratops or does her buff go through first and save her dinosaur?
answer:
The instant you casted and the instant she casted are both on the stack. According to rule 608.1, each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves. This means the order in which the instants are on the stack determines their resolution order.

In your scenario, since you casted your instant first, it is on the top of the stack. Your wife then countered it with her instant, which is now on the top of the stack. Therefore, the "Giant Growth" will resolve first because it is on top of the stack.

After "Giant Growth" resolves, increasing the Ceratops's power and toughness, then your instant will resolve, dealing 4 damage to the Ceratops. Since the Ceratops's toughness is now increased by "Giant Growth," it will not be reduced to 0 toughness and will not be destroyed by your instant.

The specific rules that apply here are:
- Rule 608.1: Each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves.
- Rule 603.4: If a triggered ability has an intervening "if" clause, it checks whether the clause’s condition is true. If it isn’t, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing. Otherwise, it continues to resolve. However, in this case, there are no intervening "if" clauses to consider.

So

The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last.

Maybe you guys can settle something for me. If I have Leyline out turn one, can my opponent use dredge with Dakmor Salvage without it getting exiled?
answer:
No, the Leyline of the Void will exile the card being dredged by Dakmor Salvage. According to rule 702.52a, "Dredge N" allows a player to mill N cards and return the card with dredge from the graveyard to their hand if they have at least N cards in their library. Dakmor Salvage, an artifact with the ability "When Dakmor Salvage enters the battlefield, exile the top card of your library. If that card is a creature card, you may put it onto the battlefield under your control," will exile the top card of the library when it enters the battlefield.

However, Leyline of the Void, an enchantment with the ability "Enchanted player may not mill cards," prevents the act of milling cards. But it does not prevent the exile of cards by Dakmor Salvage. Therefore, even with Leyline of the Void in play, the card being dredged by Dakmor Salvage will still be exiled.

question:
Yurlok of Scorch Thrash + Fiery Emancipation
Does [[Fiery Emancipation]] work with [[Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]]'s ability? As in, if I tap Yurlok for his mana (and my opponents aren't able to use it), will it then hit them for 9 damage each?
I don't believe it does as the source of the damage isn't coming from Yurlok (as in, it isn't worded "Yurlok does damage equal to the amount of unspent mana") therefore it isn't coming from a source I control.
Could you confirm if there's an interaction or not?
Thank you!
answer:
No, there is no interaction between Yurlok of Scorch Thrash's ability and Fiery Emancipation in the way you described. Yurlok of Scorch Thrash's ability does not create a source of damage that can be used by Fiery Emancipation.

Yurlok of Scorch Thrash's ability is a triggered ability that triggers when a player taps Yurlok for mana. The ability then causes each opponent to lose 9 life. However, this damage is not a result of Yurlok being a source of damage; it is a separate effect that happens when the triggered ability resolves.

The key points are:
- Yurlok of Scorch Thrash's ability is a triggered ability that triggers when it is tapped for mana (603.2e).
- The damage from Fiery Emancipation is a replacement effect that modifies the mana production event (603.12b).
- The damage from Yurlok of Scorch Thrash is not a result of the mana production, but rather a separate effect that occurs when the triggered ability resolves.

Therefore, the damage from Yurlok of Scorch Thrash is not a source of damage that can be used by Fiery Emancipation. The damage is simply a consequence of the triggered ability resolving, not a result of mana production.

question:

If a player had Rienne out and 2 other multi colored creatures and another player cast something like Blasphemous Act killing all creatures, would the multicolored creatures go back to hand?
answer: The rules do not specify what happens to creatures that are put into their owner's hand by an effect like Blasphemous Act. However, the rules do not indicate that creatures are put into their owner's hand when they are destroyed either. Typically, when a creature is destroyed, it is put into its owner's graveyard (510.10a). Since Rienne, Angel of Rebirth is not a double-faced card or a meld card, and there are no specific rules that state creatures go to the hand when they are destroyed, we must conclude that the multicolored creatures would go to their owner's graveyard, not their hand. There are no specific rules in the provided text that directly address this scenario. Therefore, based on the given rules, the multicolored creatures would be put into their owner's graveyard.

question:
Asmora... (not gonna type all that) and chainer, nightmare adept
Can i cast Asmora from the discard if i choose it with chainer. And if so how much does she cost?
answer:
Yes, you can cast Asmora, Queen of the Memes from the graveyard using Chainer, Nightmaring Chainer. According to the rules, Chainer, Nightmaring Chainer has the ability "Chainer, Nightmaring Chainer deals 1 damage to any target. You may choose to put that many cards from the top of your library into your graveyard. If you do, you may cast one of those cards without paying its mana cost." 

The cost to cast Asmora, Queen of the Memes would be 3 life, as indicated by her card text: "Chainer, Nightmaring Chainer deals 3 damage to any target. You may choose to put that much life from the top of your library into your graveyard. If you do, you may cast one of those cards without paying its mana cost." 

So, you would deal 3 damage to a target, put 3 life from the top of your library into your graveyard, and then you can cast Asmora, Queen of the Memes without paying its mana cost.

question:
Stab wound and the +1/+1
Two scenarios to make sure I understand this.
A) I have a 2/2 on the field I give it a +1/+1 counter, my opponent [stab wound] it - enchantment that gives -2/-2. Does it for or is it a 1/1
B) same 2/2 but this time I have a lord giving it +1/+1. Again my opponent stab wounds it. Dead or a 1/1?
answer:
A) The 2/2 with a +1/+1 counter becomes a 1/1. Here's the reasoning:
- The +1/+1 counter makes it a 3/3.
- Stab Wound gives -2/-2, resulting in a 1/1.
- The total power and toughness is 1, so it remains a 1/1.

B) The creature with the +1/+1 from the Lord also becomes a 1/1:
- The Lord gives +1/+1, making it a 3/3.
- Stab Wound gives -2/-2, resulting in a 1/1.

The rules for doubling and applying negative values (107.1b) apply here, but since the calculations yield a negative power and toughness, the values are capped at 0. Therefore, in both scenarios, the creature ends up as a 1/1.

question:
Celestial Dawn with Zedruu in Commander?
So I'm currently building a commander deck and was wondering about , a card that I've seen in many Zedruu builds. After talking with some friends, I was led to believe that there was a ruling within the past year or so where, in commander, a player can generate colors outside of their commander's colors. Is this true? And if so, does this make Celestial Dawn basically useless for the purpose of shutting people out of their lands? Thanks for any input!
answer:
The rules do not support generating colors outside of a commander's color identity in Commander. Specifically, rule 903.4 states that color identity is established before the game begins and is based on the mana cost or rules text of the card. Rule 903.5c further reinforces that a card can only be included in a Commander deck if every color in its color identity is also in the commander's color identity.

Therefore, Celestial Dawn, which has a colorless mana cost, cannot generate colors outside of Zedruu's color identity (which is black and red) to shut people out of their lands. The ability of Celestial Dawn to generate colorless mana and then choose a color is still limited by Zedruu's color identity.

Citing specific rules:
- 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text, plus any colors defined by its characteristic-defining abilities."
- 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."

question:
How to determine mana costs and effects with Henzie Toolbox Torre and cost reduction effects on x-costed creature spells?
Hi fellow MTGlers,
I have a rules question building upon a discussion about \.
Consider the following:
I have a Henzie (cast once) and \[\[Heartless Summoning\]\] on the board and want to blitz \[\[Exocrine\]\] for x = 5, because I want its Ravenous ability to trigger on ETB.
From the linked discussion above I assume I can blitz x spells with Henzie as long as I declare my intention to cast Exocrine with a total mana value of at least 4. For my purpose I declare my intention to cast it with a total mana value of 8 to make x equal to 5.
My assumptions are:
Henzie will reduce the cost for my spell by 1 generic mana
Heartless summoning will reduce the costs by another 2 generic mana
This would result in a total mana cost of 4 and a red.
In general: Do cost reduction effects affect effects based on x costs?
In detail:
Does Ravenouns trigger with the x costs reduced to less than 5?
Does Bio-plasmic Barrage trigger with the declared or reduced x value?
If the reduction of x costs indeed affect x-triggered abilities can I choose that Heartless Summoning would reduce the generic 2 instead of the x value?
I hope all of this makes some sense. Looking forward to your replies!
answer:
The rules do not specify that cost reduction effects directly affect the value of \(X\) in \(X\)-costed spells. Specifically, the value of \(X\) is determined at the time the spell is cast, and cost reduction effects do not change this value.

Here are the relevant rules and their implications:

1. **Determine the Total Cost of the Spell** (601.2f):
   - The total cost of the spell is determined at the time of casting, including any cost reductions.
   - Cost reduction effects apply to the total cost, not to the value of \(X\).

2. **Cost Reduction Effects** (107.3h, 107.3i, 107.3j, 107.3k, 107.3m, 107.3n):
   - These rules describe how cost reduction effects apply to the total cost of the spell, but they do not specify that these effects can modify the value of \(X\).

3. **X-Costed Spells** (107.3h, 107.3i, 107.3j, 107.3k, 107.3m, 107.3n):
   - The value of \(X\) is determined at the time the spell is cast, and cost reduction effects do not change this value.

If an object’s enters-the-battlefield triggered ability or replacement effect refers to X, and the spell that became that object as it resolved had a value of X chosen for any of its costs, the value of X for that ability is the same as the value of X for that spell, although the value of X for that permanent is 0. This is an exception to rule 107.3i.

If a delayed triggered ability created by a resolving spell or ability refers to X, X is not defined in the text of that triggered ability, and the spell or ability that created it had a value of X chosen for any of its costs, the value of X for the triggered ability is the same as the value of X for the spell of ability that created it.
107.3p. Some objects use the letter Y in addition to the letter X. Y follows the same rules as X.

Glossary:
- Ability: 1. Text on an object that explains what that object does or can do. 2. An activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”
- Activated Ability: A kind of ability. Activated abilities are written as “[Cost]: [Effect.] [Activation instructions (if any).]” See rule 113, “Abilities,” and rule 602, “Activating Activated Abilities.”
- Activation Cost: Everything that appears before the colon in an activated ability’s text. It must be paid to activate the ability. See rule 118, “Costs,” and rule 602, “Activating Activated Abilities.”

601.2f. The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It can’t be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.” If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.
601.2g. If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid.
601.2h. The player pays the total cost. First, they pay all costs that don’t involve random elements or moving objects from the library to a public zone, in any order. Then they pay all remaining costs in any order. Partial payments are not allowed. Unpayable costs can’t be paid.
Example: You cast Altar’s Reap, which costs {1}{B} and has an additional cost of sacrificing a creature. You sacrifice Thunderscape Familiar, whose effect makes your black spells cost {1} less to cast. Because a spell’s total cost is “locked in” before payments are actually made, you pay {B}, not {1}{B}, even though you’re sacrificing the Familiar.
601.2i. Once the steps described in 601.2a–h are completed, effects that modify the characteristics of the spell as it’s cast are applied, then the spell becomes cast. Any abilities that trigger when a spell is cast or put onto the stack trigger at this time. If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority.
601.3. A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows that player to cast it and no rule or effect prohibits that player from casting it.

Glossary:
- Activate: To put an activated ability onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. See rule 602, “Activating Activated Abilities.”
- Additional Cost: A cost a spell may have that its controller may pay (or, in some cases, must pay) in addition to its mana cost to cast that spell. See rule 118, “Costs,” and rule 601, “Casting Spells.”
- Alternative Cost: A cost a spell may have that its controller can pay rather than paying its mana cost. See rule 118, “Costs,” and rule 601, “Casting Spells.”
- Becomes: A word used in some trigger events to indicate a change in status or characteristics. See rule 603.2e.

question:
When does damage on the stack resolve?
Let's say I have a creature, with a shield token.
My opponent casts a spell with sufficient damage to kill my creature. He copies that spell while it is still on the stack and it does the same damage again.
Does the damage from both spells resolve at the same time, just destroying my Shield and my creature survives.
Or
Does my creature die as the 2nd set of damage kills my creature as the 1st destroyed the Shield.
answer:
The damage from both spells resolves at the same time, destroying the shield token but not killing the creature. 

According to the rules provided, specifically 615.7, prevention effects like shields work by preventing a specific amount of damage. Once the shield is reduced to 0, any remaining damage is dealt normally. 

The relevant rules are:
- 615.7: "Each 1 damage that would be dealt to the 'shielded' permanent or player is prevented. Preventing 1 damage reduces the remaining shield by 1. If damage would be dealt to the shielded permanent or player by two or more applicable sources at the same time, the player or the controller of the permanent chooses which damage the shield prevents. Once the shield has been reduced to 0, any remaining damage is dealt normally."

In your scenario, the shield prevents the first set of damage. When the second set of damage is applied, the shield is already at 0, so the remaining damage from the second spell is not prevented and the creature is killed. 

Therefore, the damage from both spells resolves at the same time, destroying the shield but not preventing the second set of damage, which kills the creature.
grounding_context:
615.7. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to a specific amount of damage—for example, “Prevent the next 3 damage that would be dealt to any target this turn.” These work like shields. Each 1 damage that would be dealt to the “shielded” permanent or player is prevented. Preventing 1 damage reduces the remaining shield by 1. If damage would be dealt to the shielded permanent or player by two or more applicable sources at the same time, the player or the controller of the permanent chooses which damage the shield prevents. Once the shield has been reduced to 0, any remaining damage is dealt normally. Such effects count only the amount of damage; the number of events or sources dealing it doesn’t matter.
615.8. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to the next time a specific source would deal damage. These effects prevent the next instance of damage from that source, regardless of how much damage that is. Once an instance of damage from that source has been prevented, any subsequent instances of damage that would be dealt by that source are dealt normally.
615.9. Some effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability prevent damage from a source of a player’s choice with certain properties. When the source would deal damage, the shield rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced and the shield isn’t used up. See rule 609.7b.
615.10. Some prevention effects generated by static abilities refer to a specific amount of damage—for example, “If a source would deal damage to you, prevent 1 of that damage.” Such an effect prevents only the indicated amount of damage in any applicable damage event at any given time. It will apply separately to damage from other applicable events that would happen at the same time, or at a different time.
Example: Daunting Defender says “If a source would deal damage to a Cleric creature you control, prevent 1 of that damage.” Pyroclasm says “Pyroclasm deals 2 damage to each creature.” Pyroclasm will deal 1 damage to each Cleric creature controlled by Daunting Defender’s controller. It will deal 2 damage to each other creature.

Related rules:
609.7b. Some effects from resolved spells and abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties, such as a creature or a source of a particular color. When the source would deal damage, the “shield” rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced. If for any reason the shield prevents no damage or replaces no damage, the shield isn’t used up.

Glossary:
- Ability: 1. Text on an object that explains what that object does or can do. 2. An activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”
- Any Target: A spell or ability may require “any target.” “Any target” is the same as “target creature, player, planeswalker, or battle.” See rule 115.4.
- Creature: A card type. A creature is a permanent. See rule 302, “Creatures.”
- Damage: Objects can deal “damage” to creatures, planeswalkers, and players. This is generally detrimental to the object or player that receives that damage. See rule 120, “Damage.”
- Defender: A keyword ability that prohibits a creature from attacking. See rule 702.3, “Defender.”

510.1e. Once a player has assigned combat damage from each attacking or blocking creature they control, the total damage assignment (not solely the damage assignment of any individual attacking or blocking creature) is checked to see if it complies with the above rules. If it doesn’t, the combat damage assignment is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that player began to assign combat damage. (See rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions.”)
510.2. Second, all combat damage that’s been assigned is dealt simultaneously. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. No player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it’s dealt.
510.3. Third, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.”)
510.3a. Any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt or while state-based actions are performed afterward are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesn’t matter. (See rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities.”)
510.4. If at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike (see rule 702.7) or double strike (see rule 702.4) as the combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step, instead of proceeding to the end of combat step, the phase gets a second combat damage step. The only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are the remaining attackers and blockers that had neither first strike nor double strike as the first combat damage step began, as well as the remaining attackers and blockers that currently have double strike. After that step, the phase proceeds to the end of combat step.

Glossary:
- Activate: To put an activated ability onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. See rule 602, “Activating Activated Abilities.”
- Active Player: The player whose turn it is. See rule 102.1.
- Assign Combat Damage: To determine how an attacking or blocking creature will deal its combat damage. See rule 510, “Combat Damage Step.”
- Blocking Creature: A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal block during the combat phase (once all costs to block, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield blocking. It remains a blocking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. See rule 509, “Declare Blockers Step.”

510.1. First, the active player announces how each attacking creature assigns its combat damage, then the defending player announces how each blocking creature assigns its combat damage. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. A player assigns a creature’s combat damage according to the following rules:
510.1a. Each attacking creature and each blocking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power. Creatures that would assign 0 or less damage this way don’t assign combat damage at all.
510.1b. An unblocked creature assigns its combat damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it’s attacking. If it isn’t currently attacking anything (if, for example, it was attacking a planeswalker that has left the battlefield), it assigns no combat damage.
510.1c. A blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it. If no creatures are currently blocking it (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If two or more creatures are blocking it, it assigns its combat damage to those creatures divided as its controller chooses among them.
Example: An attacking Elvish Regrower (a 4/3 creature) is blocked by Vampire Spawn (a 2/3 creature) and Helpful Hunter (a 1/1 creature). Elvish Regrower’s controller can assign all 4 damage to the Hunter, 1 damage to the Spawn and 3 damage to the Hunter, 2 damage to each creature, 3 damage to the Spawn and 1 damage to the Hunter, or all 4 damage to the Spawn.
510.1d. A blocking creature assigns combat damage to the creatures it’s blocking. If it isn’t currently blocking any creatures (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If it’s blocking exactly one creature, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If it’s blocking two or more creatures, it assigns its combat damage divided as its controller chooses among them.

Glossary:
- Active Player: The player whose turn it is. See rule 102.1.
- Assign Combat Damage: To determine how an attacking or blocking creature will deal its combat damage. See rule 510, “Combat Damage Step.”
- Attacking Creature: A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase (once all costs to attack, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. See rule 508, “Declare Attackers Step.”
- Battle: A card type. A battle is a permanent. See rule 310, “Battles.”
- Battlefield: A zone. The battlefield is the zone in which permanents exist. It used to be known as the “in-play” zone. See rule 403, “Battlefield.”
